xlink:href=#location /></svg> How to change a newborn’s sleep patterns</div></a></ul></div></div></div></div><div class=article-body><p>After spending nine months in a dark (and sometimes noisy) womb, your newborn has established her own sleep cycles, which feel natural to her even if they seem strange to you. Just as she lets you know she's hungry at any time of the day or night, your baby's sleep patterns may seem random at first, sometimes changing from one day to the next.<p>Babies aren't born knowing how to put themselves to sleep when they're tired or how to wake up when they're well-rested. This is all learned behavior. If your newborn sleeps like a vampire all day and is up all night long, or if she's exhibiting other common infant sleep patterns like frequent night wakings, restless sleeping, or <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/sleep-training-for-early-waking-baby>early waking</a>, it's all completely normal. Her sleep patterns will evolve as she grows.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1783290649991&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><p>In the meantime, your baby's erratic sleep patterns may mean that no one in the family is snoozing very soundly. Right now, there's probably only a sliver of light at the end of the tunnel, but it will grow brighter!<p>Here's what parents should know about <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/newborn-sleep.aspx>newborn and baby sleep</a> patterns.<p><section class=keytakeaways-c><div class=keytakeaways-c__header><div class=keytakeaways-c__header__summary-icon><img src=https://images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/redesign/key_takeaways.svg alt="summary icon" width=24 height=24></div><div class=keytakeaways-c__header__title>Key-Takeaways</div></div><div class=keytakeaways-c__body><ul><li><strong>Newborn sleep = super random. </strong>Infants usually snooze 14 to 17 hours a day, but not on a set schedule (wah!). The truth: short bursts of shut-eye, frequent night waking and vampire-like habits are completely normal.<li><strong> Change is coming… slowly. </strong>Around 4 months you'll start to notice longer periods of sleep though many babies continue to rouse at night and wake up with the birds. Hang in there by watching for sleepy signs and establishing a regular bedtime routine.<li><strong> Sleep is a learned process. </strong>Babies don't rest the way adults do — their Zzzs are lighter in nature and they need to feed in the early months. But with time, your little one will learn to soothe herself at night and string together more hours too.</ul></div></section><h2>Baby sleep patterns by age</h2><h3>Newborn to 3 months</h3><p>First, the good news for exhausted parents: <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/sleep/how-much-sleep-do-babies-need/">Newborns sleep a lot</a>, 14 to 17 hours a day, or about 70% of the time. But those snoozes come in random bursts of slumber. Your baby is not on any kind of schedule, at least not yet.<p>That doesn’t mean you can’t help your little night owl get some rest. Here are parents’ most common newborn sleep complaints and tips for solving them:<ul><li><strong>Trouble falling asleep.</strong> Your baby might be battling bedtime because she doesn't love her crib (rocking in your embrace is so much nicer), or isn't comfortable being placed safely on her back. If that's the case, try putting her down <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/sleep/how-to-put-baby-down-drowsy-awake/">drowsy but awake</a> in a snug swaddle with a pacifier, which can help her feel safer.<li><strong>Frequent night waking.</strong> Breastfed babies will need to nurse every two to three hours in the beginning, and bottle-fed babies every three to four hours, so don't expect more than a few hours of sleep at a time. Hopefully, your newborn is sleeping in your room, in her own bed, so you don't have to go far to feed her. If you're just too exhausted to keep getting up to nurse or give her a bottle, ask your partner or another caregiver to take over feeding duties sometimes so you can catch up on your rest. If your baby is older, keep in mind that gurgling and cooing at night doesn't always mean she needs to eat, so leave her for a little while and see if she falls back to sleep on her own before rushing in. And make sure your little one is awake before picking her up for the next feeding session.<li><strong>Fussiness while sleeping.</strong> If your newborn doesn't seem to get the deep sleep she needs, she might not be completely comfortable — even if her crib is perfectly appointed. Think about it: The womb was dark all the time, so she may be confused if there's light or activity around her. The solution is to make her environment as womb-like as possible for now, with blackout shades and a <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/sleep/white-noise-sound-for-babies/">white noise</a> machine to encourage dozing off. Check the room temperature too. The <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/baby-care/what-is-right-temperature-for-baby/">ideal room temp for babies is between 68 and 72 degrees Fahrenheit</a>, no matter the season. A chilly room can wake your baby up, whereas a too-warm room can be a risk factor for <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/sids.aspx>sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)</a>.<li><strong>Refusing to sleep.</strong> Just because your newborn doesn't want to fall asleep doesn't mean she's not tired. She is. Very. But being overtired can rev her up and make it that much harder to get to bed. The best way to get ahead of an <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/sleep/overtired-baby/">overtired baby</a> situation is to learn your child's sleepy cues. Some infants rub their eyes with their fists, yawn, or get extra fussy. Yours might do something else as a sign that it's time to rest. If the trouble continues, check to make sure she's also getting enough daytime sleep during her naps. A lot of that all-important dozing needs to happen during the day to prevent a sleep deficit.</ul><h3>4 to 11 months</h3><p>By 4 months, some babies will sleep for about five to six hours at a stretch. While this age isn’t “magic,” some moms and dads do notice a few more Zzzs at this point. What to Expect Community parent LRB35 says her little one, who's just over 4 months, has been sleeping for longer stretches. “She's also sleeping more solidly at night,” she adds.<div class=ad-container><span id=gptAd5track></span><div id=gptAd5 class="fast-ads content-ad" data-inview=true data-disabled=False data-adhesive=False></div></div><div><a class=app-to-web-promo href=https://wte.onelink.me/85iI/k4d5p53l target=_blank rel=noopener> <img src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/baby-tracker-sep-2024.png data-src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/baby-tracker-sep-2024.png alt="" class=app-to-web-promo__image><div class=app-to-web-promo__title>Track your baby's sleep with the What to Expect app</div><div class=app-to-web-promo__cheveron><img src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/redesign/chevron-right.svg data-src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/redesign/chevron-right.svg alt=""></div></a></div><p>Still, this doesn't mean yours has settled into a predictable cycle. If your baby is still fighting sleep, waking early or confusing night and day, it's time to review her sleep habits.<p>You can start sleep training your baby when she's 4 to 6 months old. Before that happens, try organizing your days around her sleep and wake patterns, which can help her put in longer stretches of quality sleep.<p>Here are the <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/baby-sleep-problems.aspx>top sleep problems for babies</a> in this age range and tips for how to solve them:<ul><li><strong>Trouble falling asleep.</strong> If your baby is cranky at night, chances are something's bothering her. Try a quick comfort check before putting her down: Is her belly full, is her diaper changed, and is she wearing a super-soft, tag-free sleeper? Review her sleep environment as well. Make sure the TV is off, limit interactions, and be as quiet as you can around the crib. If you do need to feed or change her, keep it low-key. Speak in a quiet, calming voice, and avoid doing anything that might stimulate her.<li><strong>Frequent night waking.</strong> Your baby still needs plenty of sleep, but less than she did as a newborn with longer stretches at night. If she's up in the middle of the night and doesn't seem cranky, she simply might not be tired. If this is the case, try cutting the length of her daytime naps. While naps throughout the day are an important part of your baby's development, shortening super long snooze stretches during the day can help her sleep for longer at night. Note that just because your <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/ask-heidi/month-9/sudden-night-wakings.aspx>baby wakes at night</a> doesn't mean she's ready to start the day. She might just be crying to burn off some steam before she goes back to sleep.<li><strong>Fussiness while sleeping.</strong> Once night falls, help your baby associate darkness with restful slumber by turning off lights where she sleeps and in the hallway outside. Also, check the room temperature. You feel restless at night when it's too cold or too warm in the room, and so will your baby, so make sure the room is between 68 and 72 degrees. Finally, don't let sudden noises keep her up. A <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/baby-products/sleep/best-baby-sound-machines/">white noise machine</a> can help block out intrusive sounds.<li><strong>Refusing to sleep.</strong> If your baby doesn't want to go down, she's tired — but maybe not relaxed enough to give in to sleep. The solution is to ease into bedtime with a soothing routine that offers plenty of time to unwind. Give her a feed and a warm bath, then put her into her jammies. Close the shades, sing, and read a book to her, then ease your little one off to dreamland. If that doesn't do the trick, consider making her days a little more active when she's awake. Give her plenty of <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/week-13/tummy-time.aspx>tummy time</a> and room to practice moving her arms and legs. Whatever activity your baby likes is great for burning energy and prepping her for a solid night of snoozing later. Finally, don't ditch naps. Napping enough during the day helps her sleep better and longer at night.</ul><h2>Baby sleep compared to adult sleep</h2><p>You know that expression "sleeps like a baby"? You really wouldn't want to. Your baby's sleep may seem anything but sound in the beginning. Here's how infant and baby sleep is different from grown-up sleep:<h3>Duration</h3><p>You need about seven to nine hours of sleep a night and probably don't have much time to nap. Your baby, on the other hand, sleeps about 14 to 17 hours in a 24-hour period as a newborn, and when she's older, around 10 to 12 hours at night plus naps.<h3>Quality</h3><p>Though infants spend much of the day sleeping, it's not the deep sleep that you might imagine. Active sleep decreases and deep sleep increases with age. Infants sleep restlessly because they spend half of it in REM sleep, a cycle in which dreaming occurs.<p>In the womb, at 28 weeks, your baby probably spent almost all her time in fussy REM sleep, which explains all that dancing around! Until your baby is 6 months old, she'll also spend about half her time in non-REM sleep, a deeper, quiet sleep that doesn't include as much twitching and movement. In comparison, adults spend only about a quarter of their snoozing time in REM sleep and about three-quarters in non-REM sleep.<h3>Night waking</h3><p>While adults can sleep straight through the night and usually don't notice when they wake up, a baby's sleep cycle is shorter by design. Her frequent cycling between REM and non-REM sleep and her physical need for overnight feedings mean she's likely to wake fully or partially several times a night.<p>The good news is that the older she gets, the more likely she is to soothe herself back to sleep. So while night wakings still happen, you might not even know it.<h3>Sweating while sleeping</h3><p>When adults sweat during sleep, they assume something's wrong. When babies sweat during sleep, it's often a sign that they're sleeping deeply.<p>While sweating is usually nothing to be alarmed about, make sure when you put your baby down to sleep that she's not overdressed and that the room temperature is between 68 and 72 degrees. If your baby is warm to the touch and seems like she might have a fever, check her temperature.<p>Track your baby's sleep and get expert tips, plus advice from other new parents, in the <a href=https://wte.onelink.me/85iI/7s0l3a5z target=_blank rel="">What to Expect app</a>.<h2>How long should you let your newborn sleep without eating?</h2><p>Newborns should <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/breastfeeding/basics/">eat as often</a> and as long as they want, so it may be necessary to wake your newborn if she's <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/sleep/can-a-baby-sleep-too-much/">sleeping too much</a> to meet her calorie and nutrient needs. Frequent feeding is crucial for your newborn's growth and development. Right after birth, babies lose up to 10% of their body weight and need to regain it quickly.<p>Keep in mind that while infants feed frequently, they usually consume tiny amounts, as little an ounce or two at a time. Portions and sleep times will both increase as your baby gets older. Here's a typical schedule for guidance:<ul><li>Newborns: feed every two to four hours<li>2 months: feed every three to four hours</ul><p>By 4 to 6 months, babies have generally doubled their weight. Many little ones this age can sleep six to eight hours (or more) at night before needing to eat, and then they'll eat every four to five hours during the day.<h2>How to change a newborn's sleep patterns</h2><p>Your newborn's sleeping patterns are difficult to change, but there's a lot you can do to make her environment more conducive to sleep, including making sure she's fed with a clean, dry diaper, checking that her room is the right temperature and she's not overdressed for sleep, and avoiding any distracting lights or sounds that could keep or wake her up.<p>By the time they're 5 months old, about half of babies will be more or less sleeping on their parents' schedule, while the other half will still be up too early, fighting sleep, or waking more often in the middle of the night, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP). In other words, topsy-turvy sleep patterns might be your norm for a while.<p>In the meantime, you might need to (temporarily) adjust your own sleep schedule to get the rest you need. When your baby is around 3 months old, you can <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/baby-sleep-schedule.aspx>try getting her on a sleep schedule</a>, and when she's between 4 and 6 months old, you can try <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/sleep/sleep-training-baby/">sleep training</a> if you want to.<p>Parenting is full of surprises, and your baby's sleep schedule is no exception. Your little one likely won't start to establish a regular sleep routine until around 8 to 12 weeks of age, and even then her sleep schedule will probably change, thanks to developmental milestones, travel, and other common disruptions.<p>However, as your baby gets older, she'll begin to sleep for longer stretches until eventually her sleep schedule will be in line with yours. Your Guide to a Calmer, Cozier Holiday Season During Pregnancy

by Heidi Murkoff, author of What to Expect When You're Expecting.
Fact-Checked by Kathleen Felton

Stocksy
"I'll be pretty pregnant during the holidays this year. How can I make the most of the season?"

What's the trick to savoring the holidays while pregnant? For many moms-to-be, it's slowing down while everyone else is speeding through the season. This holiday season growing a healthy baby-to-be is likely your top priority. So it's okay to let your friends and family know that parties, marathon shopping sessions, and long-distance travel will be taking a backseat this year (if that's what you prefer!).

Key-Takeaways
  • Prioritize rest and relaxation. This season, it’s more than okay to slow down, skip the stress, and savor the calm moments your body is asking for.
  • Let others lend a hand. Lighten your load by accepting help with chores, hosting, and holiday tasks (or just saying no thanks!) so you can focus on feeling your best.
  • Keep things simple and enjoyable. Pace yourself, indulge in your favorite festive treats in moderation, and do only what truly brings you joy.

If calm, quiet moments are at the top of your wishlist this year, skip the hubbub and treat yourself to the gift of some serious relaxation. You can:

  • Make the holidays about you — especially if this is your first baby. After you become a mom, your little one(s) will be the main focus this time of year (well, all the time, really). So spend the holidays while pregnant doing what makes you happy, whether it's cuddling on the couch with your partner, reading a great book by a roaring fireplace, or hitting up a restorative prenatal yoga class. Be self-indulgent now — before you have a little someone who'll need your constant indulging (at least for those first few months). “My husband and I are planning on having Christmas just us to relax and enjoy. Don't feel obliged to do anything you don't want to do!” says What to Expect Community mom bmcgr00.
  • Sleep, sleep, and sleep some more. Getting the shut-eye you need isn't easy with heartburn and bathroom runs interrupting your precious Zzzs. So on weekends and holidays, snooze when you can. Sleep late, take naps in the afternoon, or turn in early when it suits you — without feeling as if you should be partying hard or getting up early to battle the airport security lines. Looking for more ways to savor this special time? The What to Expect app offers guidance and support to help you feel your best throughout pregnancy.
  • Get some holiday help. Your loved ones want you to take care of yourself, so let them help you do just that. Take a backseat on the chores and cleaning this year — don't feel guilty if others clear the table or wash the dishes more often than you do. If you don't feel comfortable camping out on the couch, pitch in in spurts and take frequent feet-up breaks. Or volunteer to keep the littlest guests engaged by reading them a story (good practice for later) or playing a quiet circle game. Running yourself ragged over the holidays while pregnant won't do anyone any favors, so take it easy — you deserve it.
  • Pace yourself. Even if you give most of those holiday to-dos the heave-ho, you might still opt to buy gifts, get them wrapped, decorate a bit, and maybe bake a batch of cookies. Avoid wearing yourself out when you're pregnant during the holidays by tackling your to-do list early and focusing on one or two manageable tasks at a time. That way, you'll accomplish your goals without getting frazzled or fried. “I find lowering my expectations for each day helps. So if I only get half done of what I wanted to, so be it.” says What to Expect Community mom borntomom2.
  • Eat, drink, and be merry. Moderation is the key to enjoying the treats of the season if you're pregnant during the holidays. Of course, you'll need to skip the spiked eggnog and turn down the champagne, but there are still ways to indulge in the holiday spirit — and the goodies — without overdoing it. Have a mocktail or a mug of mulled cider, and don't deprive yourself of your mom's biscuits or Grandma's famous cookies. But keep a balance — make time (and leave room) for eating well during pregnancy, which you and your growing baby really need right now.

Here's to making the most of the holiday season during pregnancy and beyond!

baby's first holiday season. Any tips for how we should celebrate this year?"</div></div><div class="article-row row no-gutters"><div class="left col-12 col-lg-7"><div class=article-body><p dir=ltr>Having a little elf in the house makes the season even more magical, but before you go overboard with gifts and decorating, take a breath. A holiday on steroids will likely lead to less joy and more jangled nerves, for your baby and for you. <p dir=ltr>Here's why: Babies tend to get overwhelmed by too many changes to their routines and surroundings, and they aren't shy about letting you know it (with plenty of crying and tons of crankiness). A better plan: Make your baby's first <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/toddler/christmas-activities-for-preschoolers-and-toddlers.aspx>Christmas</a>, Hanukkah or Kwanzaa memorable instead of stressful with these ideas for the holidays.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1783290644936&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><h2 dir=ltr>Rein in the hoopla.</h2><p dir=ltr>Keep your baby's first holiday experiences intimate and low-key. Avoid bringing her to parties and crowded spaces. Germs and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/news/family/coronavirus-in-babies/">viruses like COVID-19</a> still pose a threat to her vulnerable immune system (and the many new faces and noises probably wouldn’t go over so well either). Of course you want to show off your snow angel, but stick to virtual holiday celebrations on FaceTime and Zoom until it’s safer to host larger, in-person gatherings. <h2 dir=ltr>Start your own holiday traditions.</h2><p dir=ltr>Your favorite holiday tradition may be wonderful, but is it baby-friendly? For example, this might not be the year to make that cross-country trip to see your parents or trudge through the snow to pick the perfect tree. <p dir=ltr>But your baby's first holiday is the perfect time to create new family traditions, like taking an evening stroll to check out the neighbors' light displays or dropping off gifts at your local shelter. Keep in mind that it's okay for traditions to change as your family does, so don't be afraid to nix (or adapt) a ritual as your child gets older.<h2 dir=ltr>Slow the flow of gifts.</h2><p dir=ltr>Gearing up with a sleighful of Christmas gifts or a present for each of the eight nights of Hanukkah? Not so fast. At this stage of the game, too many presents will confuse rather than delight your little one. Pare down the gift list to just a few toys for your baby's first holiday (and the next few seasons to come). <p dir=ltr>Then spread the gift-giving over the course of the day instead of a ten-minute frenzy in the morning. Or, consider one or two evenings of Hanukkah presents instead of all eight. If relatives go overboard with toys for your tot, stash a bunch to take out one by one over the next several months, especially when your cutie's got a case of the crankies or you're stuck indoors on an icky day. <p dir=ltr>One more thing: Keep holiday safety in mind, and keep choking hazards such as bows, ribbons, wrapping paper and small toys out of a baby's reach.<h2 dir=ltr>Think small.</h2><p>This isn't the year to whip up an <em>Iron Chef</em>–worthy holiday dinner or host an open house for the entire neighborhood. Instead enjoy the special little moments of the season — like reading <em>The Night Before Christmas</em> aloud or just cuddling on lazy winter mornings. If you slow down and relish your time together as a brand-new family, you'll be able to make your baby's first holiday season a beautiful one for everyone.<p>Wishing your baby (and you) a happy If you’re in the bathroom, you can steam up the room by running the shower before your baby’s bathtime. And have everything ready (supplies gathered, tub filled) before you undress your tot.<h2 id=hands>Get all hands on deck</h2><p>How to slip your slippery little fish into the tub without startling her? With her head resting on your arm and your palm under her bottom, hold her arm securely with your other hand. Then gently slide your baby into the tub, feet first.<p>Even when she’s <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/sit-up/" rel="">able to sit up</a>, keep one hand on her at all times. A sudden dip underwater won’t harm her, but it’ll give her a scare. (Review these <a href="//www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/first-bath/">baby bath safety tips</a> to keep down the fright factor for both of you.)<h2 id=toys>Try toys, toys, toys</h2><p>Need we say more? Distraction is a great baby bathtime strategy. Rubber ducky and other floating toys are sure to delight.<p>But there’s no need to go overboard: Various plastic containers work well too. (To prevent mold from collecting on those playthings, dry toys between baths in a mesh bag and clean periodically.) If your baby is tiring of her toys, check out these other ways to show her some <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/playroom/playtime-tips/big-fun-big-tub.aspx rel="">bathtime fun</a>.<p><div class=jw-video-player-wrapper data-video-id=ZQnilToH data-placement=Inline><div id=jw-video-player-ZQnilToH class=jw-player></div></div><div class="wbw-video__info d-flex justify-content-center mb-3"><span class="wbw-video__info__title text-center"></span></div><h2 id=tub>Ease into the big tub</h2><p>Just because your baby is physically ready (she’s sitting without any support), doesn’t mean she’s emotionally ready to graduate. Take baby steps like these:<ul><li>A few days before you upgrade, put her <a href="/baby-products/baby-care/best-baby-bath-tubs/" rel="">infant tub</a> in the empty big tub and bathe her as usual.<li>If she seems interested, let your baby play with toys in the tub without water. (For safety reasons, lay a dry towel on the bottom of the tub and always stay by her side.)<li>Consider <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/baby-bathtime-basics/bathing-with-your-baby.aspx rel="">bathing with your baby</a> until she’s used to the big tub. (Do remember to keep the bath temperature adjusted to her comfort level.)</ul><h2 id=splashing>Don’t make waves</h2><p>Splashing is a big part of your baby’s bathtime fun. If she’s game, show her how to splash or do a little light splashing next to her.<p>But for many infants, the joy comes from being the splasher, not the splashee. So, follow her lead when it comes to splashing<br>back.<h2 id=shampoo>Save the shampoo for last</h2><p>Now that you’re in the big tub, wash your baby’s hair at the end of the bath (when she’s had her fun and is more relaxed). To make rinsing less traumatic, try using a spray hose (if your tub has one) or a shampoo visor (sold in baby stores and online).<h2 id=draining>Delay draining the tub</h2><p>Ready to head ashore? Wait until your baby is out of the tub before you pull the plug. The sound of water rushing down the drain may frighten her.<h2 id=try>Try, try again</h2><p>Don’t worry if your little one doesn’t take the bait right away. Feel free to schedule bathtime just three times per week as long as you clean well during <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/diapering/how-to-change-a-diaper/" rel="">diaper changes</a>. Be patient, and before you know it, your baby’s bathtime will become a treasured part of her day.</p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. Bathing With Your Baby

by Heidi Murkoff, author of What to Expect When You're Expecting.
Medically Reviewed by Jesil Pazhayampallil, M.D., F.A.A.P.
Medical Review Policy

Is it safe to take a bath with your baby? And if so, what do you need to know before you climb into the tub with your little one?

It can be more than okay to bathe with your baby! For starters, what better way to shower your little one with love and boost bonding than to cuddle skin-to-skin? Bathing your baby in a tub of warm water can also soothe a crying jag: Your baby will probably calm down as she feels your body against hers, along with the warm water and change of scenery.

Another plus to bathing with your baby? You’re bound to get a sense of well-being, and that’s sure to wash over her. Some moms enjoy breastfeeding in the bath since the warm water can help with the letdown of milk. And taking a bath with your baby can even be a time-saver: After you’ve washed her (and snuck in a snuggle or two), hand her off to your partner and finish up with a little private tub-time.

Of course, bathing with a baby is a whole different ball game from sudsing up solo. Some things to keep in mind:

  • Wait until she’s old enough. Don’t submerge your baby in water until her umbilical cord drops off and her navel has healed. Stick to sponge baths and turn to other bonding tactics, such as kangaroo care (holding your baby’s bare body against your bare chest) until then.
  • Make sure the water is just right. It should be body temperature or a tiny bit warmer (use a thermometer if you’re not sure) and no deeper than two or three inches. It's also a good idea to set the water heater thermostat in your house to 120 F or lower to avoid accidental burns (sometimes parents add more water during the bath if it's getting cold). This is especially important when bathing with older babies and children who "want to do it themselves" and can turn on the faucet.
  • Gather everything you’ll need before you get into the tub, including any items you’ll use to bathe your baby (body wash, shampoo, washcloths, towels). If you forget something, skip it or take your baby with you if you must have it now. Never, never leave your child alone in the tub, not even for a second.
  • Step into the water sans baby. Do not try to climb into the (slippery) tub while holding your (slippery) little one. Place her in her bouncy seat or car seat beside the bath, get in yourself, and then reach over for her. Better yet, have your partner hand her to you.
  • Get a grip. If your tub doesn’t have a nonslip mat, lay one down now so that you don’t slide around: Even if you’re sitting, your baby could easily take a nosedive if you slip. And when you’re taking a bath with your baby, keep both hands on her at all times. Try bending your knees and letting your little one recline against your thighs facing you.
  • Keep her wet and warm. Use a plastic cup to pour water over your baby’s body from time to time — that’ll keep her from getting chilly.
  • Make a safe exit. When baby bathtime is over, reverse the steps you followed to get into the tub: Place your baby into her bouncy or car seat and tuck a towel around her, or hand her to someone else before you get out.

The real beauty of bathing with your baby is that it’s an experience you can share for months to come. Of course, by then, taking a bath with your little one will be more about water play than snuggling, but that’s okay.

Have a splash!

Wondering what your baby's nursing personality is? See if your little one fits into one of these categories.
Back to Top

  • Gourmet
  • Rester

Part of getting to know your infant is getting in tune with her newborn nursing personality. As you've probably already figured out, just as your baby has a unique cry and a unique way of curling into your arms, she also has a nursing style that's all her own.

But is your newborn's nursing style unique — or does it fit into the norm? Here are five major categories of nursers that can help you better understand your baby's style — and what to make of her newborn nursing habits.

Barracuda

Is your baby like a little vacuum, latching on tenaciously and suckling with all her might for 10 to 20 minutes at a time? If yes, you may have a barracuda-like baby on your hands (or at your breast!). Sure, there's no dawdling at the breast with this newborn nursing style, but the quick action that characterizes this type may cause you pain due to your infant's vigorous suck.

To prevent sore nipples, make sure your itsy-bitsy barracuda gets a good, deep latch. If you're in pain throughout the feeding, that's a sure sign that the latch needs some fixing. 

In that case, remove your hungry baby from the breast (break her suction gently and carefully by putting your pinkie in the corner of her mouth), and try the latch again until it feels right. Also, consider switching breastfeeding positions so that your baby doesn't irritate the same sore spots again and again.

Excited ineffective

You'll be able to tell if your baby is an excited ineffective if she's so thrilled to see your breast (and smell her next meal!) that she can't keep her mouth grasped around the nipple long enough to actually nurse. Once these newbie nursers lose hold of the breast, they end up screaming in frustration (which can be frustrating for you as you try to get the hang of breastfeeding).

Track every feed and pump in the What to Expect app

Your goal with this newborn nursing personality is to keep your baby calm: Prevent your little one from getting too excited (and inevitably frustrated) by offering your breast at the first sign of hunger (such as rooting or sucking on her hands). You can also try putting some breast milk on your nipple or hand expressing so the milk has already let down before you latch. That way when the baby finally latches, she gets something. 

Then do your best to create a soothing nursing environment — sit in a glider and rock your baby while she breastfeeds, offer lots of skin-to-skin contact and, most of all, try to keep your cool so that your infant doesn't get even more wound up and off her nursing game. Also, rest assured that as your baby gets older and more practiced, she'll become a more-effective (and probably less-excited) nurser.

Procrastinator

Infants with this laid-back newborn nursing personality tend to be more interested in snoozing than suckling. If your baby is a procrastinator, make sure she gets needed nutrition and regular practice breastfeeding by putting her to your breast often even if she doesn't seem hungry. (Doctors recommend eight to 12 times a day for all newborns.) You may need to wake her up to feed her.

If it's time to feed and she's still sleepy, you can undress her so she's not as warm and cozy, perking her up a bit.

Don't stress about how much your baby is drinking — newborns need very little volume early on. You'll be able to tell if your baby is getting enough breast milk by making sure that her diaper output is on track and if she seems happy and content (or drifts back to sleep) after most feedings. Soon enough, your little procrastinator will probably get her nursing act in gear.

Gourmet

These future foodies know how to savor their milk, so if your baby is a gourmet, she tends to mouth the nipple, play with it, smack her lips and take her time tasting each mouthful of milk. There's no use in trying to hurry a gourmet, since you'll only make her angry and upset. 

Instead, your best bet is to go with the flow (so to speak), and let your little one take her time. Keep in mind that even the newborn nursers who eat for the longest stretches get quicker as they get older.

Rester

How can you tell if your baby has this newborn nursing personality? Resters like to nurse for a few minutes and then rest for a few minutes, or even nod off only to wake up and want to continue nursing again — which can be quite confusing to a new mom, who is eager to have some predictability when it comes to her baby's nursing schedules.

As with a procrastinator, you can do your best to try to keep your infant alert through feedings. To that end, try unswaddling or undressing your baby while she's nursing, or tickle her feet to keep her awake. You can also manually massage your breast in order to pump some milk into your newborn's mouth when she starts to slow down her suck-swallow pattern and drift off to dreamland. The good news is that as your rester matures, she'll start to get a more-regular newborn nursing pattern

Healthy babies are born with basic motor responses, known as newborn reflexes, that help them survive and thrive in their brand new environment.<p>Some of these baby reflexes may be subtle, while others, like the Moro reflex (aka the startle reflex), are pretty hard to miss. But they're all incredibly important and tend to have a specific purpose — which is why the pediatrician will check them at your baby's <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/health-and-safety/baby-first-checkup-doctor/">first doctor's visit</a> a day or two after birth.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1783275008390&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><p>Here’s what you need to know about the Moro reflex, including what it looks like and why it happens.<h2 id=what>What is the Moro reflex?</h2><p>The startle or Moro reflex is a hard-wired response in your newborn to something unexpected — a loud noise, say, or the sensation of falling. It often happens when your baby is sleeping, but can also occur while he's awake.<p>If your baby is exhibiting the Moro reflex, you’ll know it. He’ll suddenly arch his back, fling his arms up and out, and open his hands. Then your little one will draw up his knees and bring his arms and re-clenched fists close to his body — almost as if he’s giving himself a hug. Seconds later, as abruptly as the startle started, it’s over, though your baby may also cry. <p>While it may be jarring to you at first until you get used to it, it doesn't bother your baby at all and is an indication that he's healthy and developing as he should. Think of it as your newborn’s first attempts to protect himself and regain his sense of balance.<p dir=ltr>And don't worry — the Moro reflex isn't bad for your baby and typically goes away in a few months. One downside, however, is that newborns can startle themselves awake and then have a hard time settling back down (sometimes even crying a lot as a result). But babies often aren't bothered by it at all and fall back to sleep right away, as if nothing ever happened.<div class=ad-container><span id=gptAd5track></span><div id=gptAd5 class="fast-ads content-ad" data-inview=true data-disabled=False data-adhesive=False></div></div><div><a class=app-to-web-promo href=https://wte.onelink.me/85iI/k4d5p53l target=_blank rel=noopener> <img src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/baby-tracker-sep-2024.png data-src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/baby-tracker-sep-2024.png alt="" class=app-to-web-promo__image><div class=app-to-web-promo__title>Track your baby's sleep with the What to Expect app</div><div class=app-to-web-promo__cheveron><img src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/redesign/chevron-right.svg data-src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/redesign/chevron-right.svg alt=""></div></a></div><p><div class=jw-video-player-wrapper data-video-id=Fh0sPaMT data-placement=Inline><div id=jw-video-player-Fh0sPaMT class=jw-player></div></div><div class="wbw-video__info d-flex justify-content-center mb-3"><span class="wbw-video__info__title text-center"></span></div><h2 id=last>How long does the Moro reflex last?</h2><p dir=ltr>The Moro reflex starts at birth — and in fact, your practitioners will check for it in those first hours after your baby is born. It usually lasts for a few months. While every baby is different, most parents notice their little one's startle reflex peaking in the first month and beginning to fade at around 2 to 4 months, disappearing completely by 6 months or so.<p dir=ltr>But even earlier, when your baby is about <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/month-by-month/week-6.aspx>6 weeks old</a>, he’ll start to acclimate to life on the outside and feel more secure in his surroundings (thanks to you).<p dir=ltr>In the meantime, don’t sweat the startles, as they’re a sign of healthy neurological development. But do try to offer your infant lots of extra support when you’re toting him from one place to another.  <h2 id=triggers>What triggers the Moro reflex?</h2><p dir=ltr>Just about everything is unfamiliar to newborns, so they're easily surprised and even frightened by new-to-them sensations and sounds. Here are some of the things that may trigger the Moro reflex:<ul><li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr><strong>Your newborn thinks he’s falling</strong>, like when you put your little one down in his bassinet without enough support (don’t worry, it happens)<li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr><strong>Any unexpected movement</strong>— for instance, you scoop your baby from his car seat or shift the position of his head<li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr><strong>Loud, sudden noises nearby</strong> — like a dog's piercing bark, an ambulance wailing down the street or something dropping and crashing to the floor<li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr><strong>Your baby jerks his arms or legs</strong> and startles himself<li dir=ltr><strong>Very bright lights,</strong> especially when they're flicked on in a previously dark or dim room<li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr><strong>No apparent reason at all,</strong> though if it's when he's asleep,<strong> </strong>he might have been dreaming of falling</ul><p dir=ltr>Doctors check for the Moro reflex because it’s a sign that your baby’s nervous system is working.<p dir=ltr>While your baby is on his back, the pediatrician will either gently pull on your little one's arm to lift his shoulders slightly up off the padded examining table and then let go, or slowly lift your baby's head with a hand and suddenly release it, but then support the head quickly so it doesn't hit the padded table.<p dir=ltr>Both little tests can produce the sensation of falling, and will likely cause your baby to startle or have a startled look on his face (and possibly even cry) if his Moro reflex is normal.<h2 id=stop>How to stop your baby from startling</h2><p dir=ltr>You can’t entirely get rid of the startle reflex and wouldn't want to — after all, there’s a reason Mother Nature included it with the rest of the primitive responses babies are born with. And remember that the Moro reflex does begin to fade on its own after a few months as your baby gets more used to the world and his nervous system matures.<p dir=ltr>Still, there are ways for you to help your baby stop startling awake, including:<h3 dir=ltr>Hold your baby close</h3><p dir=ltr>Babies startle when they’re jostled suddenly. So be gentle when you pick up your cutie and put him down, and try to keep his neck and head supported with your hand. You won’t always succeed in nixing the startle response, but soon you’ll become a pro at holding your baby securely.<h3 dir=ltr>Try swaddling</h3><p dir=ltr><a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/baby-care/baby-care-101/secrets-to-swaddling.aspx>Swaddling</a> is the art of wrapping your baby up in a blanket so he looks like a tiny burrito. A tight-but-not-too-tight <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/baby-products/sleep/best-swaddle-blankets/" rel="">swaddle</a> keeps him from flailing his arms and legs so he sleeps more soundly.<p dir=ltr>You can get a swaddling tutorial at the hospital or online, or make it easier by buying a swaddle blanket with Velcro tabs. You can also opt for a sleep sack or a sleep/swaddle sack instead for naptime and bedtime. Just be warned: Not all babies like being confined, so some take to swaddling better than others. And remember you'll <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/sleep/when-to-stop-swaddling-baby/" rel="">have to stop swaddling</a> if your baby is wriggling out of the blanket or showing signs of <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/roll-over/" rel="">rolling over</a> (usually around the 3- to 4-month mark), as it can pose risks for your little one.<h3 dir=ltr>Turn down the noise </h3><p dir=ltr>If you can, tread lightly and quietly around your baby, especially when he's snoozing. You can’t stifle every sound, but you can minimize the din with a <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/sleep/white-noise-sound-for-babies/" rel="">white noise</a> machine or fan until the sounds of your home and surroundings are more familiar to your newborn.<h2 id=doctor>When to call the doctor</h2><p dir=ltr>Your baby’s health care provider will probably be the one to discover if your newborn has no Moro reflex at all, or if it seems abnormal in some other way.<p dir=ltr>One caveat: Preemies often don’t have a well-developed Moro reflex or it may appear weaker, so you may not recognize it when your <a href=/first-year/having-a-premature-baby.aspx rel="">premature baby</a> startles. <p dir=ltr>But if you notice anything amiss with your baby or any changes between doctor's visits, be sure to contact your pediatrician as soon as possible. Signs to look for include the following:<ul><li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Your baby is no longer showing signs of the reflex, which might indicate some sort of brain or spinal cord damage.<li dir=ltr>Your baby can only move one side of his body, which might mean his shoulder is broken or the nerves that run down his neck to his arm are damaged.</ul><p dir=ltr>What happens if the Moro reflex doesn’t go away? Remember, babies develop at their own pace. That said, if your older baby still has the Moro reflex well past about 6 months, there may be something more serious going on. Get in touch with your pediatrician, who will be able to perform a test to find out if there's anything wrong.<p dir=ltr>In the meantime, try not to jump every time your baby jumps! Those startles are a good sign, even if they do come with some cries. Soothing your baby will make him feel more secure, and pretty soon, the Moro reflex will be a thing of the past.</p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. to overstimulation</div></a></ul></div></div></div></div><div class=article-body><p>All parents-to-be dream of having an easy, content baby who coos and smiles on cue and cries only when she's hungry or needs her diaper changed. Reality usually does a number on that particular fantasy.<p>Most babies sob more (and sleep less) than they do in parental dreams. That's because <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/week-10/decoding-cries.aspx>infants cry to communicate</a> their needs and express their feelings.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1783293368694&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><p>But while most babies cry — and startle — in response to stimuli in their environment, some highly sensitive babies seem to be more easily, and intensely, set off. You can chalk this up to a child's temperament; a sensitive baby is born that way. A wet diaper, a bright light, a rough label on the neckline, a whistling kettle and a scratchy blanket can all unduly upset a baby whose senses (one or all) are easily overloaded.<p>If you have an extra sensitive baby, your best bet is to avoid things that bother her and keep (as much as you can) the intensity of sensory stimulation around her down. Here are some of the most common culprits that can set a sensitive baby off and what you can do to <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/care/how-to-make-baby-stop-crying>stop crying</a> before it starts.<h2 id=noise>If your baby is sensitive to noise </h2><p>If noise seems to upset your sensitive baby, use a soft voice when you speak or sing to her, steer clear of loud toys and lower the volume of (or turn off) music, the TV and your phone's ringtone when she's awake.<h2 id=light>If your baby is sensitive to light</h2><p>Dim the lights (or use shades) in your baby's room and keep visual stimulation to a minimum. Avoid the TV and choose toys that are muted in color and design.<h2 id=touch><strong>If your baby is sensitive to touch</strong></h2><p>Change your baby's diaper often and dress her in comfortable clothing. Cotton knits with smooth, nonirritating seams, snaps, labels and collars are ideal.<p>Cover <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/baby-products/sleep/best-crib-sheets rel="">crib sheets</a> with blankets while your baby's not sleeping so the sheets aren't too chilled when she's ready for bed, and keep bathwater and room temperatures at levels she seems to like best.<h2 id=stimulation>If your your baby is sensitive to overstimulation </h2><p>Handle your sensitive baby gently, avoid big crowds and reduce daily activities (read: one baby class, not three).<p>Limit the number of playthings you give her. Rotating between one or two toys at a time should help.<p>Talk to your baby's doctor if you have any concerns, but keep in mind that many babies outgrow this sensitive-to-everything phase once they've adjusted to the hectic pace of life on the outside. In fact, some mellow out once the <a href="//www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/health-and-safety/what-is-colic/">colicky</a> months are over, usually around <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/month-by-month/month-3.aspx rel="">3 months old</a>.</p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. care that no amount of parenting classes can prepare you for: cleaning your first diaper blowout, sucking snot from plugged-up infant nostrils and the sheer amount of baby spit-up you’ll encounter.<p dir=ltr>About half of all babies spit up at some point during their early lives. While it might feel concerning to see your little one spitting up — you're probably wondering whether she's actually keeping enough breast milk or formula <em>in</em> her stomach — know that spit-up is normal and expected.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1783293370433&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><p dir=ltr>Keep reading for the full lowdown on baby spit-up, plus when to talk to your doctor if you're concerned about how much your little one is spitting up.<h2 id=why>Why do babies spit up?</h2><p dir=ltr>Baby spit-up, or the dribble of stomach contents that can come out after feeding, is messy, frustrating … and perfectly normal.<p dir=ltr>An infant's digestive system is still developing, and her lower esophageal sphincter — a ring of muscle that keeps food in the stomach — isn’t fully functional for several months. This makes it very easy for food that she’s just eaten to come back up. If your baby's stomach is very full after a feeding or you’ve changed her position suddenly after eating, for example, that can force food out of her stomach and up her esophagus in the form of spit-up.<p dir=ltr>Babies also might spit up when they burp, drool, cough or cry. The fact that your infant is on an all-liquid diet (you know, breast milk or formula) also makes it easy for the contents of her stomach to come right back up.<p dir=ltr>In very rare cases, your baby’s formula might be contributing to excessive spit-up. According to the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), an estimated 5 percent of babies have milk-soy protein intolerance, meaning that they cannot properly digest the proteins present in milk- or soy-based formulas. (Spit-up is one of several signs that could indicate this condition.) If your baby is diagnosed with this condition, her doctor might recommend a hydrolyzed formula.<h2 id=causes>Possible causes for baby spit-up</h2><p dir=ltr>Although spit-up is normal, there are a few reasons why your little one might be emptying the contents of her stomach.<h3>Spit-up </h3><p dir=ltr>Normal spit-up looks a lot like whatever baby is eating, which is either breast milk or formula before she starts solids (usually sometime around 6 months). Both breastfed and formula-fed babies spit up, and the act of spitting up usually looks effortless. It often comes out through the mouth and/or nose, but doesn’t cause pain and isn’t forcefully done. In fact, most babies typically don’t mind or notice spit-up. <h3>Reflux<strong> (infant GERD)</strong></h3><p dir=ltr>Technically, spit-up is reflux. But sometimes, if it's accompanied by other symptoms or poor weight gain, spit-up might indicate that your baby has a condition called gastroesophageal reflux disease in babies, also known as <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/childrens-health/infant-gerd/">infant GERD</a>.<p dir=ltr>With infant GERD, the lining of the esophagus becomes irritated and damaged by all the spit-up. It can cause pain and fussiness during and after feeding, and make it harder for baby to feed and gain weight. Other signs of GERD include excessive drooling, uncontrollable crying, poor sleep and erratic feeding patterns. Talk to your child's pediatrician if you notice these symptoms.<h2 id=vomit>Baby spit-up vs. vomit: How can you tell the difference?</h2><p dir=ltr>Spitting up and vomiting might seem similar. They’re both messy, and both involve your baby’s stomach contents ending up on your clothing.<p dir=ltr>But unlike spit-up, vomit is forceful (and in more serious cases, even projectile). It is also caused by a virus, bacteria, food poisoning or some other kind of specific health issue. Sometimes, vomit can be green (which hints that there might be an infection) or red (which indicates there’s some kind of blockage or gastrointestinal bleeding). Other causes of baby vomit might be motion sickness, certain prescription medications, or disturbing sights or sounds.<p dir=ltr>In rare cases, true vomiting might indicate that your baby has something called pyloric stenosis, which is when a muscle in the stomach thickens, preventing food from moving to the small intestine. This can cause projectile vomiting and dehydration, and needs to be treated immediately. Symptoms typically start when baby is between 2 weeks and 2 months old.<h2 id=normal>How much baby spit-up is normal?</h2><p dir=ltr>Yes, spit-up means laundry day happens a lot more often during baby's first few months of life. But it’s usually perfectly normal. And while you might feel like your baby is spitting up all her breast milk or formula, that is usually not the reality.<p dir=ltr>Some babies rarely ever spit up; others spit up after nearly every meal. And volumes of spit-up can vary.<strong> </strong>Most often, spit-up is a mix of food and stomach acid, and it’s hard to quantify how much is actually coming back up — which is why doctors rarely use volume on its own to tell whether spit-up is normal or a sign of something more serious.<p dir=ltr>Instead, doctors typically consider the following when assessing a baby’s spit-up: <ul><li dir=ltr>Is the spit-up forceful? <li dir=ltr>Is it colored red or green?<li dir=ltr>Does baby appear to be uncomfortable or in pain?<li dir=ltr>Is baby still feeding normally? <li dir=ltr>Is baby still gaining weight normally? </ul><p dir=ltr>Those kinds of questions help practitioners figure out whether a baby is spitting up normally or if something else might be contributing. But as long as your baby is still otherwise healthy and gaining weight, spit-up is likely normal.<strong><br></strong><p dir=ltr>Some parents also wonder if it's typical for babies to spit up hours after eating. While spitting up typically happens during or shortly after a feeding, if your baby is otherwise healthy, happy, gaining weight and doesn't have any of the red flags above, this is also probably normal, but ask your child's pediatrician if you have any concerns.<h2 id=stop>When do babies stop spitting up?</h2><p dir=ltr>Spit-up happens in most infants, so know that it’s normal — and it gets better as they get older!<p dir=ltr>Babies typically spit up until they’re around 12 months old. You can expect spit-up to get more frequent until about <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/month-by-month/month-3.aspx rel="">3 months of age</a>, and then it should gradually start to get better as baby gets stronger and can sit up on her own.<p dir=ltr>However, if your baby starts spitting up for the first time after 6 months of age or her spit-up turns to vomiting, that could be a sign that something more serious is going on.<h2 id=tips>Tips to minimize spitting up in babies</h2><p dir=ltr>To prevent spitting up from happening as often, there are a few steps experts typically recommend.<ul><li dir=ltr><strong>Don’t overfeed. </strong>Babies’ stomachs are small, and it’s easy to overload them. (This tends to be more of an issue with bottle-fed babies, since it’s easier for babies to get milk from a bottle nipple than from the breast.) Try feeding more often at smaller volumes if you notice that your baby often spits up during feedings.<li dir=ltr><strong>Hold baby upright for 30 minutes after feeding. </strong>Sitting chest-to-chest on you for at least a half hour after each feed might minimize the amount of spitting up your baby does.<li dir=ltr><strong>Burp frequently. </strong><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/baby-care/how-to-burp-your-baby/">Burping</a> gently during and after feeds — for bottle-fed babies, at least once halfway through a feeding or after every 2 or 3 ounces, and when you switch from one breast to the other for breastfed babies — can help reduce spit-up.<li dir=ltr><strong>Limit post-feeding activity.</strong> Going straight from a feeding to playtime might cause milk to come back up, for example.<li dir=ltr><strong>Use a slow-flow nipple. </strong>If you bottle-feed, try using a slow-flow nipple. These are designed to slow down feeding and reduce the amount of air baby takes in while eating — which may help reduce spit-up risk. </ul><h2 id=doctor>When to call the doctor about baby spit-up</h2><p dir=ltr>Spit-up is usually normal and healthy. But in rare cases, your baby’s spitting up habits might indicate a more serious health problem. Be sure to talk to your doctor if you notice any of the following: <ul><li dir=ltr>Not gaining weight well or losing weight<li dir=ltr>Crying or arching her back while feeding<li dir=ltr>Refusing to feed<li dir=ltr>Spit-up that starts after 6 months or continues past 18 months<li dir=ltr>Yellow, green or red spit-up<li dir=ltr>Frequent forceful or projectile vomiting <li dir=ltr>Spit-up accompanied by other symptoms such as bloody stools, wheezing or coughing, fewer wet or dirty diapers, lethargy and/or fever </ul><p dir=ltr>Like dirty diapers, spit-up is a normal part of early parenthood. While you should keep an eye out for any abnormal symptoms, spit-up is usually something to ride out. In the meantime, thank goodness for <a href="/baby-products/baby-care/best-burp-cloths/" rel="">burp cloths</a> and stain removers! </p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. class="page-main-content maincontent clearfix"><div class="row no-gutters"><div class="col-12 deck">Find out why it's impossible to spoil a newborn with your love and attention.</div></div><div class="article-row row no-gutters"><div class="left col-12 col-lg-7"><div class=article-body><p dir=ltr>Whether it’s from a family member or a well-meaning neighbor, almost every new parent has heard the same warning at some point or another: “If you keep picking up your baby every time she cries, you’re going to spoil her.” Or, “Watch out — you can spoil a newborn by feeding her whenever she wants.”<p dir=ltr>To those who say you pay too much attention, don’t pay them any attention (true for much of the unwanted <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/community-new-mom-tips/">baby advice</a> you’ll be getting). The truth is, it’s impossible to spoil a newborn. That’s right, impossible! And the experts agree. Here’s what the research shows:<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1783293372028&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><h2 dir=ltr>Newborns cry because they have basic needs</h2><p dir=ltr>Their needs are actually the same as their wants at this age — to be fed, held, comforted and loved. And it is your job to listen to your instincts and respond to those needs and wants as best you can. If that means toting your infant around in a sling while you do the laundry or getting up every few hours throughout the night to nurse, so be it. That won’t spoil a newborn — far from it.<p dir=ltr>When you respond to <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/week-10/decoding-cries.aspx>your newborn’s cries</a> and try to meet her needs, you’re teaching her to feel secure and confident. And that security and confidence will result in less crying and more independence in the long run. That’s because young babies who feel a deep trust in their parents tend to develop a secure sense of self that helps them self-soothe later on.<h2 dir=ltr>Newborns aren’t manipulative</h2><p dir=ltr>Worried that your baby may be using her whimpers and tears to manipulate you? Even your precious angel isn’t smart enough for that kind of complicated thought at this young age. Newborns’ needs and wants are much more straightforward.<p dir=ltr>So each time you or your partner quickly responds to your infant’s cries for food, a cuddle or help nodding off to sleep, you’re reinforcing the notion that you’ll be there for your little one and that she can count on you. This notion will not spoil a newborn but will instead help her <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/ask-heidi/week-1/postpartum-bonding.aspx>develop a healthy bond</a> with her parents.<p dir=ltr>Of course there will be times when you can’t get to your infant as quickly as you might like (hey, parents have to pee, too!), but responding to your infant’s needs as best you can will let your infant know she’s loved. And guess what? A baby who’s secure in her bond with her parents is a happier, less-needy baby — and becomes an older baby who has the courage to take on the world without clinging to you.<h2 dir=ltr>It's a little different with older babies</h2><p dir=ltr>Once your baby gets to be about <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/month-by-month/month-6.aspx>6 months old</a>, however, her wants will get more sophisticated and they may not be the same thing as her needs. For instance, an older baby may <em>want</em> to <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/ask-heidi/baby-hair-pulling.aspx rel="">pull your hair</a> or earring or she may want that TV remote with all the interesting buttons. <p dir=ltr>In cases like that, it’s good to set some consistent limits and <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/baby-behavior/teaching-discipline.aspx>teach discipline</a>. Use different toys to distract her and replace objects she shouldn’t play with. And offer positive words instead of negative ones as much as possible, like “This is how we pet a cat” instead of “Don’t pull Fluffy’s tail!” That way, your baby will eventually learn the concept that you don't always give her what she wants, but you still love her.<p dir=ltr>For now, though, while your little one is still so young, remember that you can’t spoil a newborn — but you can teach her to trust in you and the world.</p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. class=article-body><p>Your baby is mobile, or nearly so! That’s exciting, but it’s also the beginning of a whole new level of trouble when it comes to making mischief. But your baby isn’t deliberately trying to make messes, or risk his life and limbs (and yours…and the cat’s). He’s simply finding new ways and new opportunities to explore his environment, a sure sign of intelligence and security.<p>While he once stayed put on his blanket, playing with his toys, he can now make his way into more dangerous territory. So what’s on the agenda these days? In addition to <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/nursery-decorating/childproofing-basics.aspx rel="">baby-proofing your home</a>, you also have your first chance at teaching discipline.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1783293373554&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><h2 id=teach>Can you teach discipline to a baby?</h2><p dir=ltr>Babies are naturally curious — after all, everything around them is new and different. Your little one is eager to explore his surroundings — which is a good thing! — but as your baby approaches his first birthday, you can start to teach him that some of these surroundings can be dangerous and are off-limits.<h3 id=no>When do babies understand "no"?</h3><p>At about 9 to 10 months, your baby’s memory improves, making him more receptive to new learning. So where your choruses of “No!” and “Hot!” and “Dangerous!” once went in one cute little ear and out the other, he can now <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/toddler/understand-directions/" rel="">begin to recall your words</a>, actions and tone of voice from one day to the next.<p>Introducing discipline at this stage helps you start to teach lessons about right versus wrong, caring and respect for others, self-control and safety. True, these are pretty big concepts, and helping your baby learn them will take years, but that’s all part of growing up.<h2 id=how>How do you discipline a baby?</h2><p>Also known as the rules for making rules:<ul><li><strong><strong>Don’t always say "no." </strong></strong>Babies understand that “no” means “no” around 9 months if used firmly and consistently. But consistent use is not the same as overuse. Save “no” for dangerous behaviors such as touching the stove or going near electrical sockets. <li><strong>Do redirect him. </strong>Picking your baby up and placing him in another location, giving him a toy or taking away a toy are all good ways to indicate that it’s time for a change. When you want your baby to stop doing something undesirable, employ language like “stop” or “don’t do that” followed by redirection.<li><strong>Do tell and show your baby how much you love him. </strong>Remember, you’re correcting his behaviors, not him. Model politeness and respect (with him and everyone else!).<li><strong>Don’t be too strict or rigid. </strong>If you set your standards too high, it’s hard for your little one to feel like he can succeed and develop the self-control he needs to behave even when out of your sight. But…<li><strong>Do be strict enough. </strong>Setting limits that are fair helps him feel loved and protected — boundaries teach safety. If you’re overly permissive, he may get the sense that you don’t care what he does.<li><strong>Don’t let down your guard about safety. </strong>You might be teaching your baby that the stove is hot or the stairs are steep, but don’t count on him to avoid temptation.<li><strong>Do take personality into account. </strong>Some babies require a firm tone of voice, while others respond better to a gentler one. Still others must be physically removed from a dangerous area before they get the message. And circumstances (like <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/ask-heidi/introducing-new-babysitter.aspx rel="">introducing a new sitter</a> or an <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/teething/" rel="">erupting tooth</a>) matter too when it comes to getting your message across.<li><strong>Don’t shame, criticize or strike your child. </strong>Disciplining a child is sometimes as difficult for parents to do as it is for children to receive, but it's important to manage your emotions.<strong> </strong>Your baby isn’t trying to be cruel to the cat by pulling her tail; he’s just curious about what will happen when he does. Children, and especially babies, are not intentionally trying to be cruel or malicious. Responding to behavior by spanking, shaming or criticizing can lead to <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/toddler-behavior/aggressive-behavior.aspx rel="">issues of aggression</a> or lack of confidence later in life. <li><strong>Do be consistent. </strong>Telling your baby not to climb up on a chair one day, then letting him do it the next is confusing. So is saying “don’t touch” without following up if (when!) he ignores your request. It takes a lot of patience and repetition to teach adherence.<li><strong>Do catch him being good. </strong>Praise him for offering a toy to a little friend or for “helping” you with a chore. Accentuating the positive is truly powerful!</ul><p><em>Additional reporting by <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/authors/nikeshaelise-williams-1535 rel="">Nikesha Elise Williams</a></em></p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>.
