cue ball you’d imagined. In fact, it may be downright pointy or mysteriously misshapen. Or it may sport a soft spot that pulses with every heartbeat. (All this and you’ll still think he’s adorable.) <p dir=ltr>Here’s a rundown on how your baby’s head shape may change in those first months of life.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1783293375066&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><h2 id=causes>What causes changes to a baby’s head shape?</h2><p dir=ltr>Several different factors can affect your baby’s head shape, which may appear cone-shaped, asymmetrical or have a flat spot on one side: <h3 dir=ltr>Birth</h3><p dir=ltr>At birth, a baby’s head has an average circumference of 13.8 inches and makes up about a quarter of the length of his body. (Imagine that ratio on a grown-up!) So how does a baby’s huge noggin make it through the birth canal? You can thank the <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/ask-heidi/baby-soft-spot.aspx>fontanelles, or soft spots</a>, on your newborn’s head.<p dir=ltr>Fontanelles are the membrane-covered gaps between several bony plates making up the skull. They helped your infant’s head to shift and mold so it could fit through the birth canal. And if you’ve had a vaginal delivery — especially one in which you had to push for a long time — that head may appear <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/newborns/conehead-baby/">pointy or cone-shaped</a>, thanks to the time spent squeezing through. <p dir=ltr>The fontanelles also give your baby’s brain room to grow (very!) rapidly during his first year. The largest soft spot is on top of your newborn’s head, called the anterior fontanelle, can measure up to 2 inches across. It’ll start to close when your baby is about 6 months old and close completely (forming a solid skull) by the time he reaches 18 months. <h3 dir=ltr>Positioning</h3><p dir=ltr>Placing babies on their backs to sleep is one of the most effective ways to reduce the risk of <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/sids.aspx rel="">sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)</a>. The not-so-nice by-product of the “back to sleep” campaign: <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/health/plagiocephaly-flat-head-syndrome/">flat spots that appear on baby’s head</a> if he always rests in the same position — a condition known as positional plagiocephaly, to get technical. <p dir=ltr>Spending lots of time lying flat in a car seat, stroller or rocker can similarly lead to a flat spot on part of the head. And babies who experienced extra cramped conditions in the womb (often twins or multiples) may be born with a flat spot on the head too. <h3 dir=ltr>Congenital torticollis</h3><p dir=ltr>Sometimes an asymmetrical baby head shape (flattening on one side of the head) is due to <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/congenital-torticollis>congenital torticollis</a>, a normally mild condition characterized by limited neck mobility. Tight conditions in the womb, like if your baby is in the breech position, can affect the way the neck muscles develop. <p dir=ltr>Babies with torticollis have a difficult time moving their head to one side. That means that baby’s head shape may become more asymmetrical over time if your baby usually sleeps or rests with his head facing his preferred side. <h2 id=worry>Should you worry about baby’s head shape?</h2><p dir=ltr>In nearly all cases (and especially with treatment), your baby’s head shape will eventually become a non-issue. Here’s what you should keep an eye out for:<ul><li dir=ltr><strong>Soft spots.</strong> Your baby’s soft spots are totally normal and much less fragile than they seem, since they’re covered by strong membranes that safeguard the brain. Two (rare) signs of trouble: A <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/newborns/sunken-fontanel-soft-spot/">sunken fontanelle</a> could signal dehydration, and a constantly bulging one could indicate pressure on the brain. In either case, contact your baby’s doctor. Also let your doctor know if your baby’s fontanelles haven’t started to shrink within one year. <li dir=ltr><strong>Conehead.</strong> You can expect your baby’s head to round out within a few days to weeks of birth. If you’re concerned, ask your doctor, who can rule out other potential (rare) causes and recommend treatment if necessary to help your baby’s head take a rounder shape.<li dir=ltr><strong>Flat spots.</strong> Almost all flattened areas are minor and disappear by the time a child is 2 years old, especially if you carefully follow your doctor’s recommendations. <li dir=ltr><strong>Congenital torticollis.</strong> Your pediatrician will likely diagnose your baby within the first few weeks and suggest special exercises and maybe physical therapy. In the rare case that your baby’s head shape is still severely asymmetrical after a year, a special muscle-release surgery may help.<strong><br></strong></ul><h2 id=treatments>Treatments for baby’s head shape</h2><p dir=ltr>If your newborn’s head is misshapen from his journey down the birth canal, your doctor may very well take a wait-and-see approach, as a cone shape will likely go away on its own without any treatment within a couple of weeks.<p dir=ltr>Otherwise, the treatment for baby’s head shape depends on the cause. It may involve:<h3 dir=ltr>Tummy time</h3><p dir=ltr>One of the best ways to prevent and treat a misshapen head is to make sure your baby gets plenty of <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/week-13/tummy-time.aspx>supervised tummy time</a> when he’s awake. Working your way up to 15 minutes (or more) of tummy time per day helps to strengthen your baby’s neck muscles, as well as develop motor skills that will one day help your baby <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/crawling/">learn to crawl</a>. <h3 dir=ltr>Switching up baby’s sleep position</h3><p dir=ltr>You should always place your baby to sleep on his back to help prevent SIDS. But it’s a good idea to vary his sleep position (laying him down with his head at alternate ends of the crib) — especially if he has a misshapen head for any reason. This ensures he doesn’t always rest in the same position, which helps keep one side of his head from flattening.<h3 dir=ltr>Holding your baby</h3><p dir=ltr>When your baby is awake, try to keep him out of the bouncer, stroller, car seat or carrier as much as possible and carry him in your arms instead, to relieve pressure on his head. <h3 dir=ltr>Helmets or bands</h3><p dir=ltr>If your child has a flat spot or cone-shaped head that doesn’t resolve on its own, your doctor may recommend that he wears a special medical helmet or band and refer you to someone properly trained to measure and fit one. These devices apply gentle pressure to redirect the skull’s growth. <p dir=ltr>Your doctor will likely recommend that your baby sport the helmet all day and night long, taking it off only for bathing. For most babies with flat spots, therapy ideally starts at around 5 or 6 months of age (and before 12 months) and usually lasts for about three months.<h3 dir=ltr>Stretching exercises and physical therapy</h3><p dir=ltr>If your little one has an asymmetrical head shape due to congenital torticollis, your doctor may show you some stretching and strengthening exercises to help lengthen and loosen your baby’s neck muscles, and you may see a physical therapist for more guidance.<h2 id=permanent>When does baby’s head shape become permanent?</h2><p dir=ltr>Your baby’s largest fontanelle should close by around <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/milestones/13-18-months/" rel="">18 months</a> of age, and your child’s head will reach about 90 percent of its adult size by his second year! That means most abnormalities in a baby’s head shape should disappear by the time a child is 2 years old. <p dir=ltr>Between <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/baby-care/baby-skin-care/cradle-cap.aspx>cradle cap</a> and a cone-shaped head, you wouldn’t be the first parent to think your child looks a little alien when he’s first born. Rest assured, nearly all of these quirks resolve within the first days to weeks after birth — and certainly within the first year or two. Still, don’t hesitate to bring up any concerns with your baby’s doctor. Your pediatrician can ensure you’re taking all the steps to help ensure your baby’s noggin takes on the round shape you expect.</p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. child's height?</div></a></ul></div></div></div></div><div class=article-body><p>Gazing into your newborn's eyes, it’s tough to imagine that tiny face (and those teensy hands and feet) will one day be about as big as yours.<p>And while it’s impossible to know what your baby will look like when she grows up, there is one thing you might be able to predict while she’s still relatively little: her future height.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1783293376873&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><h2 id=factors>Factors that affect your child's future height</h2><p>A number of factors are at play in determining your child's height as an adult, including:<h3><strong>Genetics</strong></h3><p>As you might guess, heredity has a lot to do with how tall your baby will be, accounting for about 80 percent of your baby's height. If you and your mate are tall, chances are you’ve got a kid who’ll one day need extra-long pants too.<h3><strong>Sex </strong></h3><p>The average American man is 5.5 inches taller than the average American woman, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). <h3><strong>Exposure to smoke</strong></h3><p><a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/smoking-cigarettes-during-pregnancy/" rel="">Smoking cigarettes during pregnancy</a> has been shown to reduce the height of an expecting woman's baby.<h3><strong>Nutrition</strong></h3><p>Having not enough to eat or eating very poorly — especially within the first 1,000 days of life, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) — can make kids deficient in the vitamins and nutrients they need to grow. And that can permanently stunt a child’s growth and decrease adult height.<h3><strong>Exercise</strong></h3><p>Most kids don’t get nearly enough exercise — but a child who participates in extremely intense exercise at a young age can have a slowed or changed growth pattern.<h3><strong>Medical conditions</strong></h3><p>A number of very rare conditions can also affect a child’s adult height, including:<ul><li><strong>Turner syndrome,</strong> a chromosomal disorder that results in short height and is usually apparent by about age 5.<li><strong>Gigantism,</strong> a disorder where an excess of growth hormone during childhood causes kids to be larger than other children their age.<li><strong>Dwarfism,</strong> where kids grow to an adult height that’s under 4 feet due to genetic disorders or other medical conditions. The most common type of dwarfism, achondroplasia, accounts for 70 percent of all cases and is detected either in utero or shortly after birth.<li><strong>Childhood growth hormone deficiency,</strong> a disorder where the pituitary gland does not make enough growth hormone, resulting in slow or flat rate of growth. While it’s sometimes noticed at birth, it may not be diagnosed until a child is 2 or 3 years old.<li><strong>Chronic childhood illnesses</strong> like severe arthritis, untreated celiac disease or cancer may slow a child's growth.<li><strong>Chronic use of some medications,</strong> especially corticosteroids, can impede a child's growth.</ul><h2 id=how>How to figure out how tall your child will be</h2><p>While no test is 100 percent accurate, once your child is 2 years old, his doctor can begin to predict his adult height using the following methods:<h3><strong>X-rays</strong></h3><p>Also known as the Bayley-Pinneau scaling law, a doctor uses an X-ray of a child’s hand and wrist to determine skeletal age (also called bone age). By comparing this information to historical data, doctors can make fairly accurate predictions of adult height.<h3><strong>Khamis-Roche method</strong></h3><p>In the mid-1990s, a doctor and a statistician teamed up to find a simpler solution than X-rays. They developed the Khamis-Roche Method, a mathematical formula that you can begin to use once a child is 4 years old. <p>Simply plug in a child’s current weight, height, age and parents’ adult heights to predict your little one's eventual adult stature. A calculator does the rest — no radiation required. While it may not work for exceptionally tall kids, it is the most accurate predictor without getting an X-ray.<h3><strong>Mid-parental height method</strong></h3><p>Most kids grow to about 2 inches of what’s known as their parents’ "mid-parental height," which finds the average of parent’s heights using different formulas for boys and girls. The formula can give you a good idea of your child's height, though it's not an exact science.<ul><li><strong>For boys,</strong> adult height is calculated by combining both parents’ heights, dividing by two, then adding 2.5 inches.<li><strong>For girls,</strong> you’d add both parents' heights together, divide by two, then subtract 2.5 inches.</ul><h3><strong>Doubling height at age 2</strong></h3><p>While there aren’t studies verifying the accuracy of this popular method, it’s a quick way to give curious parents an idea of what to expect. So much growth happens during the toddler years that kids generally reach half of their adult height within the first two years of life. <p>Simply doubling your boy’s height at <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/toddler/24-month-old.aspx rel="">2 years old</a> and your girl's height at <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/toddler/18-month-old.aspx rel="">18 months</a> (since girls tend to develop faster than boys) gives you a rough guesstimate of your child's future stature. <h2 id=why>Why predict your child's future height?</h2><p>How tall your child will be is not just a fun tidbit of information. Once you and your doctor know your child’s estimated adult height, you won't worry so much when the inevitable <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/ask-heidi/baby-growth-spurts.aspx rel="">growth spurts and plateaus of childhood</a> and adolescence happen.<p>And if your child is consistently shorter than the trend for her predicted adult height, your doctor can explore whether an undiagnosed illness or nutritional deficit is to blame.</p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. bleeding</div></a></ul></div></div></div></div><div class=article-body><p dir=ltr>Your baby’s umbilical cord stump is a funny little piece of skin that’s actually the last link to his stay in the womb. When the umbilical cord is cut at birth, a bit remains still attached to his navel — and it’ll go through a metamorphosis during your baby’s early days.<p dir=ltr>Indeed, the color and look of the stump changes from yellowish-green to black and crusty as it dries up and then falls off. Frankly, it looks downright weird, even gross, but don't be intimidated. Read on for easy care tips for your baby’s umbilical cord as well as what to do if you think something’s not right.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1783293378469&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><h2 id=when>When does the umbilical cord fall off?</h2><p dir=ltr>It may seem like it’s taking its sweet time, but the <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/cut-umbilical-cord>umbilical cord</a> stump should dry up and drop away by the time your baby is 3 weeks old, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP). <p dir=ltr>It’s possible the stump will fall away sooner, but if it’s lingering longer than that timeframe, make an appointment with the pediatrician to get it checked out. <h2 id=do>What to do when the umbilical cord falls off </h2><p dir=ltr>Most cords dry completely and then fall off, leaving behind a cute baby belly button. You might notice a small raw spot or a bit of blood-tinged fluid oozing out. Try not to worry — this is also normal. But if you notice more profuse bleeding, call the doctor. <p dir=ltr>In some cases, the cord may form reddish-pink scar tissue called <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/newborns/umbilical-granuloma>an umbilical granuloma</a>, which may secrete a yellowish discharge. This should clear up in a week, but if it doesn't, check in with your baby’s pediatrician. An umbilical granuloma is a very treatable condition.<h2 dir=ltr>Umbilical cord care tips</h2><p dir=ltr>Nowadays, the standard practice when it comes to caring for a newborn umbilical cord is to keep it dry. Skip the rubbing alcohol and other ointments, and follow these umbilical cord tips to promote good healing:<ul><li dir=ltr><strong>Keep it clean. </strong>If the stump gets dirty, dab it gently with a wet washcloth and then pat the area with a dry cloth. (It's unlikely you'll need to do this, as the cord usually stays pretty clean.) Avoid using soap, which can irritate a baby’s tender skin. <li dir=ltr><strong>Air the stump out.</strong> Help the base dry by regularly exposing it to air.<li dir=ltr><strong>Stick to sponge baths. </strong>Don't dunk that navel underwater for now — sponge baths are enough. Once the stump falls off, feel free to <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/first-bath/">bathe your baby</a> in his pint-sized tub.<li dir=ltr><strong>Diaper delicately. </strong>Avoid covering the stump with the top of his diaper. Some newborn-size disposables feature a little notch at the waistband, or you can simply fold down the front of the diaper to keep it from rubbing the stump area.<li dir=ltr><strong>Change diapers frequently.</strong> Change wet and dirty diapers promptly so they don't leak upward toward the navel and aggravate your baby’s healing cord.<li dir=ltr><strong>Dress delicately too. </strong>Choose loose-fitting clothing that doesn't press against the stump or outfits with a special cutout for this area. Instead of onesies that snap at the crotch, try kimono-style bodysuits, which tie on the side for more air circulation and less rubbing.<li dir=ltr><strong>Resist touching or pulling. </strong>Let the scab fall off on its own. Never pull it, even if it seems to connect by only the tiniest thread. If it gets yanked off too soon, it could start bleeding continuously. If this happens, call your baby's doctor immediately.</ul><h2 id=infection>Infected umbilical cord or belly button</h2><p dir=ltr>Healing belly buttons almost always look worse than they actually are, even when they're progressing normally. It's rare that a healing umbilical cord stump gets infected, but when it does, the condition is called <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/healthy-and-safety/omphalitis>omphalitis</a>.<p dir=ltr>Watch for these symptoms of a newborn belly button infection, or omphalitis:<ul><li dir=ltr>Red skin or a red, swollen appearance at the base of the cord<li dir=ltr>A fluid-filled lump on or near your baby's umbilical cord stump<li dir=ltr>Oozing pus or discharge<li dir=ltr>Bleeding from the scab (though a little dried blood is normal)<li dir=ltr>Foul smell <li dir=ltr>Fever or lethargy<li dir=ltr>Low appetite<li dir=ltr>Abdominal swelling<li dir=ltr>Crying when you touch the cord or the area around it</ul><p dir=ltr>If you notice any signs of infection or your baby seems to be in pain, call your pediatrician. A course of antibiotics will get your baby’s belly button back to healing in no time. <h2 id=bleeding>Umbilical cord or belly button bleeding</h2><p dir=ltr>It’s normal to spot a few drops of blood on your baby’s diaper after his stump falls off, but you should monitor any additional umbilical cord bleeding closely. Contact your baby’s doctor if a small amount of bleeding lasts for more than three days.<p dir=ltr>If heavier belly button bleeding won’t stop after 10 minutes of direct pressure applied two times or if there’s a blood stain that’s more than two inches across, immediately call or visit the pediatrician. Continuous bleeding or a sizable spot of blood at this very young age (under a month) is a concern and should get checked out.<p dir=ltr>Less is more when it comes to caring for your baby’s umbilical cord. If you keep the stump area dry and you do your best to avoid touching it when you diaper and dress your baby, this little piece of leftover skin should fall off in no time at all.</p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. Knowing how to dress the newest member of your family for extreme temperatures can seem a little confusing at first, but remember that if you’re cold, chances are your baby is cold, and if you’re hot, well, you get the drill.<p>Whether the temperature dips below freezing or it’s in the triple digits, it’s all about layers that you can add or remove as needed. Here’s everything you need to know about preparing for any weather scenario with your new baby.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1783270037865&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><h2 id=cold>How to dress a newborn for the cold</h2><p>No matter the reason you have to <a href=/first-year/protecting-kids-from-extreme-cold rel="">brave the cold with your baby</a>, just make sure your little one is bundled up well. These tips can help:<ul><li><strong>Think layers.</strong> It’s always best to layer <a href="/baby-products/best-baby-clothes/" rel="">baby’s clothing</a>, which traps heat between the layers. Thin cotton clothes work well, starting with a thin sleeper onesie and then adding as needed — maybe a long sleeved shirt and pants or even a <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/baby-products/baby-clothes/baby-snowsuits rel="">snowsuit</a> if your little one is going to be in very cold temps.<li><strong>Cover up.</strong> Make sure that your baby is completely covered from head-to-toe. If you need mittens, gloves, a hat, thick socks and boots, make sure your baby is wearing them too.<li><strong>Don’t forget to use blankets outside.</strong> If you’re headed out in the stroller, you can use a blanket and/or your stroller’s rain cover as a plus-one layer; they can keep out the elements and keep in some heat.<li><strong>Abide by car seat safety.</strong> Once you get to the car, remove baby’s bulky coat because it can compress below the harness and be too loose in the event of an accident. He can still wear multiple thin layers as well as a hat and mittens in the car seat.<li><strong>Beware of overheating.</strong> Babies dressed in too many layers of blankets or clothing are at greater risk for overheating and <a href=//www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/sids.aspx>SIDS (sudden infant death syndrome)</a>. If you’ve been out, remove your baby’s winter clothes as soon as you come inside (yes, even if he is asleep!).<li><strong>Keep the room temperature cool.</strong> Putting your sweetie to bed or down for a nap? In the winter or summer, try to keep the room temperature between 68 and 72 degrees Fahrenheit. To make sure your baby is comfortable, check his neck to see if he’s too sweaty. A little dampness goes with the baby territory, but pools of perspiration definitely do not.<li><strong>Skip the blankets at nap and bedtime.</strong> Dress him in a warm sleeper or <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/baby-products/sleep/best-sleep-sacks/" rel="">sleep sack</a>, but skip the blankets. Loose bedding is also a risk factor for SIDS.</ul><h2 id=hot>How to dress a newborn for hot weather</h2><p>Overheating isn’t just a cold-weather condition — <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/health-and-safety/how-to-protect-children-from-extreme-heat/">hot and humid days can also be dangerous for newborns</a>, who can’t yet regulate their own body temperature. Here’s how to keep your little one safe:<ul><li><strong>Take away layers.</strong> When the temperature is over 75 degrees F, a single layer should be enough for baby.<li><strong>Cover baby's head with a lightweight hat.</strong> Cold or hot, hats are important to protect baby from too much sunlight.<li><strong>Think thinner.</strong> When it’s really warm outside, use lighter fabrics, especially at night. Baby will likely still require one more layer, which can include a light sleeper onesie and a thin sleep sack. Once babies <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/roll-over/" rel="">roll over</a>, they no longer require a sleep sack. If you’re wearing your newborn in a sling or carrier, be sure the material is breathable so your little passenger doesn’t get too hot.<li><strong>Keep baby shielded from the sun.</strong> Most doctors support <a href="//www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/sunscreen-for-babies/">using sunscreen on babies</a> of all ages, although the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) doesn't endorse the use of sunscreen on babies under 6 months old. For newborns, it’s really best to avoid sun exposure completely in hot or cold weather. Make sure shade is available if you’re headed to the beach, and limit your time in the heat to a few minutes at a time, especially at midday when the sun is strongest.<li><strong>Protect those peepers.</strong> Make sure that baby’s eyes are protected from the sun with 100 percent UV protection sunglasses. (You can also try dressing your baby in UV clothing to protect her skin!)</ul><h2 id=mild>How to dress a newborn for warm or cool weather</h2><p>When the temperature is mild, it’s still best to use the layer rule. Dress baby in as many layers as you require and then add one more.<p>Also, make sure that your little one is always dry because wet or damp clothing can make baby cold even when the weather is just cool. And check his diaper frequently when you’re outside.<p>Additionally, no matter the temperature, make sure that your baby is shielded from the sun by his car seat or stroller canopy, a hat, sunglasses or just shelter.<h2 id=temperature>What's the right temperature for baby?</h2><p>Whatever the weather is like outside, <a href="//www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/baby-care/what-is-right-temperature-for-baby/">your baby’s temperature</a> should always be between 98 and 100 degrees F; a rectal reading is always the most accurate. When it’s out of the normal range, that may be a sign of illness.<p>What’s more, whether it’s summer or winter, baby’s nursery should stay between 68 and 72 degrees F. If your baby is preterm, keep the thermostat a bit higher at 72 degrees F.<p>If it’s too hot, it can increase a baby’s risk of SIDS. If it’s too cold, it can cause a risk of hypothermia, when your little one’s temperature drops to a dangerously low level. When your baby is sick and has a fever, dress him in lighter, acrylic fabrics.<h2 id=signs>Signs it's too hot or cold for baby</h2><p>When babies are too warm, they may look flushed and sweaty or they may breathe rapidly. This can cause them to be cranky and irritable and, in more extreme cases, lead to <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/health-and-safety/how-to-protect-children-from-extreme-heat/" rel="">heat stroke</a>.<p>If your baby seems overheated, start to remove layers, head inside and then call your pediatrician or 911 if he does not cool down immediately.<p>When your baby is too cold, he may develop frostbite or hypothermia. Check for signs of lethargy or unresponsiveness. If <a href=//www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/baby-care/baby-skin-care/frostbite.aspx>baby has frostbite</a>, the affected area may appear blistered and white or pale gray. In both cases, contact your doctor immediately or call 911.<p>Whether it’s frosty cold or scorching out, it’s all about keeping your baby comfortable and protected from the elements. Think layers and follow your gut. If you’re nervous that your baby is too hot or too cold, make a wardrobe adjustment ASAP or head inside to enjoy some temperature-controlled comfort.</p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. class=article-body><p dir=ltr>Once upon a time, a cardinal rule of <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/month-1>newborn care</a> was that new parents and babies should hole up inside their homes for weeks after birth. Today, we know that it’s perfectly safe to take your newborn on an outing from day one (or two, or three — whenever she’s released from the hospital or birthing center). If you’re up for it, chances are she will be, too.<p dir=ltr>But because viruses, including the coronavirus, are becoming a fact of life, you’ll want to take some extra precautions when you’re out and about with your newborn. Along with these added safety measures, remember to <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/baby-health-and-safety/dress-newborn.aspx>dress your baby for the weather</a> so she’s warm enough, but not too hot, and protect her delicate skin from the sun’s rays (even on cloudy days) with a hat.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1783293381101&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><p dir=ltr>Start slowly with your outings so neither of you gets overtired. Stash diapers, wipes, an extra blanket and a change of clothes in your bag or stroller, so you have all your supplies on hand. For more on taking a newborn outside and in crowds, as well as the latest COVID-19 advice, read on.<h2 id=when>When can I take my newborn outside? </h2><p dir=ltr>As mentioned, you can head out the door on day one with your newborn if she’s properly dressed, you avoid very extreme weather and you stay out of direct sunlight. Babies and their new parents benefit from a change of scene (yup, it’s boring when you’re cooped up inside all day), so a short stroll on your block or a feeding session on a park bench is a nice respite.<p dir=ltr>When it comes to planning a meet-up with friends and family, they’re probably as excited to get to know your newborn as you are to show her off. But because of COVID-19, the best advice is to restrict visitors, both inside your home and out until the pandemic is behind us. Blame your pediatrician or your own motherly instincts, but get your message across.<p dir=ltr>As for the people who do live in your home, don’t allow your baby near anyone with COVID-19 symptoms or possible virus exposure. Be especially careful with young siblings, and teach them to gently pat the baby’s back, or touch her tiny toes, but never her hands or face. And after any outing or family hug session, clean your baby’s hands with a wipe or wet, soapy cloth. <h2 id=covid>Is it safe to take my newborn outside during the COVID-19 pandemic? </h2><p dir=ltr>Yes, it’s fine to walk outside in the fresh air, but because the COVID-19 pandemic is ongoing, it’s critical that you avoid crowds and maintain a safe, physical distance with your newborn. It’s also important that every adult — outside of your immediate household — washes his or her hands well, wears a face covering or mask and avoids touching the mask, too.<p dir=ltr>Some places, such as doctors’ offices, offer parents the option of waiting in the car before an appointment or bringing newborns through a separate entrance and then waiting in a space where they can be safely distanced from other families. If you can avoid it, skip the grocery store, restaurants and other indoor venues where ventilation may be poor, and it can be difficult to socially distance from others.<h2 id=crowds>How can I keep my newborn safe in crowds? </h2><p dir=ltr>Keeping your newborn safe in crowds is best done by avoiding all crowds, period. If you must go to a place where there are lots of people, wear your baby in a sling, wrap, age-appropriate carrier or keep her in a stroller so others don’t get too close. Stay physically distanced as much as possible, wash hands often and wear a mask (infants, however, should not don face coverings).<p dir=ltr>It pays to be extra careful for the first month — the younger your baby, the less time her immune system has had to strengthen. (This is especially important for infants born prematurely or with other health concerns.) In normal times, before COVID-19, pediatricians would generally allow an outing in a crowd after the baby received her vaccine round at 2 months of age.<p dir=ltr>Still, this advice can vary from doctor to doctor as infants remain susceptible to viral illnesses that are not preventable with vaccines. (This is why washing hands and staying away from sick people is so prudent). Not only do newborns have a more difficult time fighting off certain illnesses, such as respiratory infections, but they are at a higher risk for serious bacterial infections. That’s why any fever (or abnormally low temperature) has to be thoroughly investigated. <h2 id=dressing>How should I dress my newborn safely for outings? </h2><p dir=ltr>Dressing your baby safely for an outing means paying attention to the weather, of course, but don’t be tempted to place a mask or face covering over her mouth and nose as a way of protecting her from COVID-19. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) warn that children under 2 should not wear a face covering due to suffocation risk.<p dir=ltr>Instead, keep her at a safe distance from others when you’re outside, and be sure that any adults you encounter are wearing masks themselves. <h3 dir=ltr>Dressing a newborn for cold weather</h3><p dir=ltr>When it’s cold out, your newborn will be most comfortable in layers of clothing, such as a long-sleeve undershirt, cozy pajamas or a one-piece outfit and a warm jacket. Older babies should wear one more layer than an adult would in the same weather conditions. Warm booties (or boots if your baby is older), as well as a cozy hat and mittens are also necessary. <h3 dir=ltr>Dressing a newborn for hot weather</h3><p dir=ltr>In hot weather, over 75 degrees Fahrenheit, your baby will only need a single layer of clothing or one more layer than you’d wear at the same temperature. Clothing with a tight weave or that’s made with UV-protective material are the best picks for bright, sunny days. <p dir=ltr>Babies under 6 months should not be in direct sunlight, so use your stroller’s canopy, an umbrella or stick to the shady side of the street. Always protect your baby’s sweet head with a hat that has a three-inch brim to cover her face, ears and neck, and apply a <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/sunscreen-for-babies/">baby-safe, broad-spectrum sunscreen</a> 30 to 50 SPF on all areas of exposed skin (for babies 6 months and up) and a minimal amount on small areas like the face (for babies under 6 months)<h2 id=friends-family>When can my newborn see friends and family?  </h2><p dir=ltr>As mentioned, most doctors will okay visits to see family and friends after the month-2 round of vaccines, but because COVID-19 is still among us, the recommendation is to stay home with your own immediate family and not socialize with others. But while we need to remain apart, this doesn’t mean we can’t take advantage of technology in order to connect with loved ones.<p dir=ltr>Try to engage by using FaceTime, Zoom and phone calls so you can show off the newest member of your family. And if friends and relatives want to support and help you, instead of allowing in-person visits, you can encourage them to drop off meals or other necessities, so you can shelter in place until it’s safe to mingle again.</p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. Here are the basics on jaundice in newborn babies.<h2 id=what>What is jaundice in babies?</h2><p dir=ltr>Jaundice is a common, short-term condition in newborns that turns a baby's skin and the whites of the eyes yellow. Jaundice occurs in about 60 percent of all babies born full-term and about 80 percent of babies born prematurely when a chemical called bilirubin builds up in the baby's blood.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1783293382891&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><p dir=ltr>The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends that all newborn babies have their bilirubin levels measured before leaving the hospital, with follow-up appointments scheduled as necessary based on the measured levels, their gestational age and other factors.<span id=1-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#1 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#1>American Academy of Pediatrics</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Clinical Practice Guideline Revision: Management of Hyperbilirubinemia in the Newborn Infant 35 or More Weeks of Gestation</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=1-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[1]</a></sup> <p dir=ltr>Most cases show up two to three days after birth and are caught by these <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/health-and-safety/newborn-screening-tests-and-procedures/">in-hospital screens</a>, while others can appear later. Jaundice usually goes away on its own (or sometimes with mild treatment) with no ill effects. It usually lasts a week to 10 days, sometimes longer for premature babies. <h2 id=causes>What causes newborn jaundice?</h2><p dir=ltr>Jaundice in a <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/newborn/" rel="">newborn baby</a> is caused by excess levels of bilirubin, a condition known as hyperbilirubinemia. Bilirubin is an substance that's produced in the blood when the body breaks down old red blood cells.<p dir=ltr>Since a newborn's liver is underdeveloped, the bilirubin often doesn't get eliminated as efficiently, which can cause the skin, and sometimes the whites of the eyes, to turn yellow.<p dir=ltr>If your baby has jaundice, you'll be able to notice the yellow tinge of her skin by gently pressing on her forehead or chest and watching the color return.<p dir=ltr>There are various causes for newborn jaundice depending on type:<h3 dir=ltr>Physiologic jaundice due to an underdeveloped liver </h3><p dir=ltr>This is the most common type of jaundice, affecting 50 percent of all newborns. Why is it so common? A newborn's liver needs a little extra time to mature and get rid of the bilirubin in her body.<span id=2-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#2 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#2>American Academy of Pediatrics</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Jaundice in Newborns: Parent FAQs</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=2-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[2]</a></sup> <p dir=ltr>Some experts call this type of jaundice a "normal" response in the first few days of life; it usually disappears within a week or two. This type of jaundice is very common in preemies, as their livers may not be fully developed.<h3 dir=ltr>Breast milk jaundice due to interference with liver function </h3><p dir=ltr>Though relatively rare, about 10 percent of breastfed babies develop jaundice when a protein in breast milk blocks the liver's processing of bilirubin, causing elevated levels. It's rarely harmful, but still requires a doctor's evaluation in case some other cause is in play. A case can last anywhere from three to 12 weeks.<h3 dir=ltr>Jaundice due to breastfeeding problems or malnutrition </h3><p dir=ltr>This type of jaundice occurs in about 5 to 10 percent of newborns due to low breast milk and calorie intake while a new mom and baby are getting acclimated to breastfeeding. While breastfeeding is still recommended for newborns who have jaundice, certain babies with this type of jaundice may require supplementing with pumped breast milk or formula in a bottle. <h3 dir=ltr>Jaundice from hemolysis </h3><p dir=ltr>This rare but serious type of jaundice begins within the first 24 hours after birth. Several different things can cause what's called hemolytic disease of the newborn. Sometimes the baby's blood type does not match the mother's or their Rh factors are incompatible. In other cases, a hemoglobin disorder (G6PD deficiency), bleeding or infection can cause early jaundice.<p dir=ltr>Prenatal testing looks to prevent this condition. Moms-to-be who are Rh-negative will likely be treated with a RhoGAM injection because their Rh factor is negative and incompatible with the baby's.<h3 dir=ltr>Poor liver function</h3><p dir=ltr>Again, this type of jaundice is rare but serious. The main clues that something is off are light gray or pale yellow stools in a newborn with jaundice that doesn't go away. It's caused by an infected liver (hepatitis) or blockage of the bile ducts of the liver (biliary atresia).<h2 id=symptoms>What are the symptoms of jaundice in a newborn baby?</h2><p dir=ltr>Although there isn't anything you can do to prevent jaundice, it's important to watch for the telltale signs and symptoms, especially since the condition may not develop until after you bring your baby home from the hospital. That way, you can seek treatment if necessary.<p dir=ltr>Some symptoms of newborn jaundice are:<ul><li dir=ltr>Yellowing of the skin and eyes<li dir=ltr>Pale-colored stool<li dir=ltr>Dark (tea- or cola-colored) urine</ul><p dir=ltr>Jaundice often appears on the face first and then spreads to the rest of the baby's body, including the chest, tummy, arms, legs and whites of the eyes. A good way to check is to place your baby in natural sunlight or under fluorescent lights and gently press her forehead and nose with your fingers.<span id=3-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#3 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#3>Mayo Clinic</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Infant Jaundice</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=3-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[3]</a></sup><p dir=ltr>If the skin appears yellow where you made the impressions, <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/week-11/call-the-pediatrician.aspx>call your pediatrician</a>. The doctor will probably want to examine your baby and take a blood sample to look at the bilirubin levels in her blood.<p dir=ltr>Jaundice can be harder to see in babies with darker skin. In darker-skinned babies, the yellowing may be more visible on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, so check there. Also look at the pink skin inside your baby's mouth in the gums and inner lips.<h2 id=risk>What are risk factors for jaundice?</h2><p dir=ltr>While most babies have mild jaundice, some are at a greater risk, including:<ul><li dir=ltr><a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/having-a-premature-baby.aspx>Babies born prematurely</a> (before 37 weeks) or at a <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/health/low-birth-weight-baby rel="">low birth weight</a> <li dir=ltr>Babies who lost a lot of weight right after delivery or had a lot of bruising or bleeding under the scalp related to labor and delivery<li dir=ltr>Babies with a parent or sibling who had a high bilirubin level and received light therapy<li dir=ltr>Babies who aren't breastfeeding well (because of poor latch, low milk supply, etc.)</ul><p dir=ltr>If you're breastfeeding, feed your baby every two to three hours, or about eight to 12 times a day. Feeding this often helps keep your baby's bilirubin level down. If you're having trouble breastfeeding, ask your baby's doctor, nurse or a lactation specialist for help. It takes time to get the hang of it.<h2 id=treated>How is newborn jaundice treated?</h2><p dir=ltr>If there are moderate to high levels of bilirubin detected in your baby, the pediatrician may recommend  phototherapy treatment, which exposes the baby to a certain type of light via a special blanket or pad. Using "bili blankets" at home or hospital helps to break down bilirubin, making it easier for the body to eliminate.<p dir=ltr>(Because of newborns' substantial risk of sunburn with direct sunlight exposure, doctors these days do not recommend putting your baby in the sun.)<p dir=ltr>Your pediatrician may also tell you to feed your baby as often as possible, without overfeeding, to encourage frequent bowel movements. That will also help get rid of the excess bilirubin, which gives stools a brownish-yellowish color.<p dir=ltr>In the most extreme form of jaundice, when bilirubin levels are abnormally high, the chemical can build up in the brain. Left untreated, very severe jaundice can lead to an extremely rare condition called kernicterus, which can result in permanent brain damage.<p dir=ltr>Measuring all babies' bilirubin levels after birth helps ensure that these very uncommon instances of kernicterus are not missed.<p dir=ltr>If your baby has more severe jaundice, she may need treatments such as:<ul><li dir=ltr><strong>Phototherapy treatment (also called light therapy or bili lights).</strong> Your baby will be undressed and put under special lights, but fear not: The lights don't hurt. Sometimes, you may need to bring your baby back to the hospital for treatment under the bili lights. <li dir=ltr><strong>Supplementing breast milk with formula.</strong> This is done on a case-by-case basis at the recommendation of your pediatrician and can sometimes help lower the bilirubin level and prevent the need for phototherapy. <li dir=ltr><strong>Red cell exchange transfusion.</strong> This treatment is called upon if bilirubin levels are abnormally high. In an exchange transfusion, your baby's blood is replaced with fresh donor blood or plasma. The need for this treatment is rare.<li dir=ltr><strong>Intravenous immunoglobulin (also called IVIg).</strong> This is a product made up of antibodies that can be given intravenously (through a vein). This is also only used rarely.</ul><h2 id=long>How long does it take for newborn jaundice to go away?</h2><p dir=ltr>Typically, jaundice goes away in a week to 10 days, though it sticks around for longer in premature babies.<p dir=ltr>If your baby is breastfed, jaundice can last a month or occasionally longer. If your baby is formula-fed, jaundice typically clears up within two weeks. If it lasts three weeks or longer, be sure to call the doctor for a follow-up.<h2 id=prevented>How can newborn jaundice be prevented?</h2><p dir=ltr>There's no way to prevent the most common type of newborn jaundice. Most cases occur because a baby's liver is not mature enough to get rid of bilirubin in the bloodstream.<p dir=ltr>You can reduce your baby's risk of jaundice by:<ul><li dir=ltr><strong>Getting a <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/rhogam-shot-for-rh-negative-moms>RHo-GAM shot</a>, </strong>if your blood type is identified as <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/pregnancy/pregnancy-health/prenatal-testing-rh-factor/">Rh-negative during pregnancy</a> and again 72 hours after delivery if your baby is Rh-positive. <li dir=ltr><strong>Feeding your baby at least eight to 12 times a day,</strong> which helps her have regular bowel movements and removes bilirubin from her body. </ul><p dir=ltr>Though it's important to watch for the symptoms of jaundice and talk to your pediatrician right away if you suspect your baby could have it, take comfort in the fact that in most newborns, jaundice is an extremely treatable, manageable and mild condition that will likely go away in a matter of weeks.</p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. squeals with delight? Nothing brings on a baby's giggles like a few aerial stunts performed in the adoring hands of those who love her. But before you send your little one flying, make sure you're playing it safe.<h2 id=type>What type of play is unsafe for babies?</h2><p dir=ltr>Certain kinds of play can be risky, especially depending on your baby's age. Infants and young children, particularly those under 2, should be played with gently to prevent unintentional injury and falls.<div id=WhatToExpect_Slideshow data-primis-ad style=margin-top:20px;margin-bottom:20px><script>(function(){function loadPrimis(){var s=document.createElement("script");s.type="text/javascript";s.src="https://live.primis.tech/live/liveView.php?s=121100&cbuster=1783293384950&playerApiId=WhatToExpect_Slideshow";document.getElementById("WhatToExpect_Slideshow").appendChild(s);}
if(window.WTEAdInfo){loadPrimis();}else{window.addEventListener("WTEAdInfoReady",loadPrimis,{once:true});}})();</script></div><p dir=ltr>Little children and especially young babies have large heads in proportion to their bodies, <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/lift-head/" rel="">weak neck muscles</a>, and fragile, still-developing brains. Infant <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/ask-heidi/baby-soft-spot.aspx rel="">skulls are also relatively soft</a> and malleable at birth (which helps her make her way through the birth canal).<p dir=ltr>All this means that babies and toddlers are more prone to serious injuries from falls or even playful games where her head may whip back and forth. And never, ever vigorously shake your baby.<p dir=ltr>Any type of shaking can lead to injury in a baby or child and is known as abusive head trauma (AHT). AHT includes shaken baby syndrome (SBS),<span id=1-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#1 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#1>American Association of Neurological Surgeons</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>Shaken Baby Syndrome</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=1-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[1]</a></sup> a serious form of abuse that usually occurs when a parent or other caregiver shakes a baby in anger or frustration.<p dir=ltr>Violent shaking in children of any age can cause severe brain damage or death, and infants and young toddlers are particularly susceptible. <p dir=ltr>The actions found in typical play (bouncing her on your knee, or tossing her in the air and catching her), don't fall under the definition of shaken baby syndrome, but can be risky. Gentle play is the order of the day.<div class=ad-container><span id=gptAd5track></span><div id=gptAd5 class="fast-ads content-ad" data-inview=true data-disabled=False data-adhesive=False></div></div><div><a class=app-to-web-promo href=https://wte.onelink.me/85iI/v98mzyc9 target=_blank rel=noopener> <img src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/my-journal-sep-2024.png data-src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/my-journal-sep-2024.png alt="" class=app-to-web-promo__image><div class=app-to-web-promo__title>Document every new milestone in the What to Expect app</div><div class=app-to-web-promo__cheveron><img src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/redesign/chevron-right.svg data-src=//images.agoramedia.com/wte3.0/gcms/redesign/chevron-right.svg alt=""></div></a></div><h2 id=tips>Tips for safe baby play</h2><p>Not sure what's safe and what isn't when it comes to playing with your baby? Here's a checklist of tips to follow:<ul><li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Never shake a baby or child.<li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Avoid any play in a young infant that involves jostling her unsupported head or neck.<li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Flipping and tossing games pose a risk for falls, which are particularly dangerous for children under 2. These games can also potentially whip the head back and forth, causing discomfort or injury. So avoid these kinds of games and make sure you always support your baby's head and neck in any game or activity you play with your little one.<li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>If you're jogging, push baby in a stroller; never run with her in a <a href="/baby-products/baby-carriers/best-baby-carriers/" rel="">baby carrier</a>.<li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Avoid pulling, jerking or lifting her by the arm, or even swinging her by the arms, to avoid potential partial dislocation at the elbow, also called “nursemaid’s elbow.”<li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Provide her with a safe, childproofed environment to explore.<li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Play on the floor as much as possible. Avoid playing on elevated surfaces such as couches or beds to avoid falls.<li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Gentle bouncing may be okay for older babies and toddlers, as long as it doesn’t scare her, put her at risk, or make her uncomfortable. </ul><h2 id=safe>Safer ways to play with your baby</h2><p dir=ltr>Having fun with baby is not only important for her development, it also offers opportunities to bond. For stress-free and safe playtime, stick to gentle games such as "flying" — holding your baby securely and gliding her through the air. Or engage her in cuddlefests or chasing games once your baby is old enough to <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/crawling/">crawl</a>. <p dir=ltr>Don't spend time worrying about past rough-housing sessions. If your child hasn't shown signs of an injury, she hasn't been hurt. If you have any concerns, however, always check with your doctor.<p dir=ltr>Here are some safe ideas for playtime with babies at every age:<span id=2-modal class=citation-tooltip href=#2 style=display:none> <span class=citation-modal-content> <span class=citation-modal-header>Trusted Source</span><span class=citation-modal-source><a class=wte-no-reset href=#2>American Academy of Pediatrics</a></span><span class=citation-modal-title>The Power of Play - How Fun and Games Help Children Thrive</span><a class="citation-modal-see-sources wte-no-reset" href=#sourceAccordion>See All Sources</a> </span></span><sup id=2-inline class=citation><a href=javascript:void(0)>[2]</a></sup> <h3 dir=ltr>Birth to 6 months</h3><ul><li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Your baby may have started smiling, so smile back! It might seem simple, but it counts as playing to a baby this young.<li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Imitate coos, and have pretend, make-believe conversations. <li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr><a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/week-13/tummy-time.aspx>Tummy time</a> is essential for developing neck and upper body strength. Get down on the floor and interact with your baby during her sessions. Talk to her and place a toy, book or mirror in front of her. Encourage her to reach for it.<li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Hold your baby and show her the world from different positions, narrating as you go.<li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Introduce sizes, shapes and colors, and let her handle safe toys (i.e. nothing too small that could be swallowed).</ul><h3 dir=ltr>7 to 12 months </h3><ul><li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Ensure that your baby's environment is safe for exploration and properly childproofed as she starts to crawl around.<li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Hold a mirror up to her cute little face and watch her watch back. <li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Play a baby favorite game like peek-a-boo.</ul><h3 dir=ltr>1 to 3 years</h3><ul><li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>She’s a toddler now and ready to conquer the world! Engage her curiosity with blocks, empty containers and puzzles. <li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Pretend play is an important way for toddlers to learn. Provide plenty of simple and safe toys for her to mimic what you do! Play along and pretend with her. <li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Read with your toddler. Name the pictures she shows interest in, describe what you see, and ask questions. <li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Sing songs, say rhymes and play different rhythms on tupperware, pots and pans.<li dir=ltr><p dir=ltr>Take your tot outside and explore together. Help her learn about movement through jumping, walking and standing on one leg.</ul><h2 id=babyproof>How to babyproof your home for playtime</h2><p dir=ltr>Keeping your baby out of harm’s way while entertaining her may have been relatively easy during those early months — you could carry her from room to room, put her down on a blanket or activity mat, and know she’d stay put.<p dir=ltr>But once she turns into a master of mobility — and always on the verge of crawling toward trouble (“What’s that small shiny thing on the rug?”) — you’ll have to double your efforts in the safety department. <p dir=ltr>Even though you may have already childproofed the house, take another look around. Pay particular attention to the rooms where your baby hangs out the most and <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/nursery-decorating/childproofing-basics.aspx>babyproof those areas</a>.<p dir=ltr>You want to give her plenty of supervised freedom to play and explore without you hovering over her every second. The best way to do that is to ensure your baby's play area is safe.<p dir=ltr>While you’re checking every room (cushioning sharp corners with corner covers, stashing away the tempting remote control, taking the house plants off the floor, tucking an extension cord behind the couch) make sure you don’t forget to do an inspection of the bathroom. Your baby has probably outgrown her infant bath and is ready to <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/playroom/playtime-tips/big-fun-big-tub.aspx>try the big tub</a>. Just keep in mind some safety rules — like never leaving your baby alone, ever! — and then break out some fun tub toys.<p dir=ltr>Remember that guidelines apply to toys, too, so keep a few <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/baby-products/educational-toys-for-toddlers/">toy-safety tips</a> in mind when you’re considering what playthings to buy for your little one. (Tip number one: Read and heed those warning labels!)<h2 id=frustrated>What to do if you're feeling frustrated</h2><p dir=ltr>Being a parent is incredibly rewarding, but it can also be difficult and exhausting. All parents get frustrated sometimes.<p dir=ltr>Even if you do everything right, <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/care/how-to-make-baby-stop-crying rel="">babies will sometimes cry</a>. If you feel yourself getting frustrated, put your child down in a safe location like the crib and step away to collect yourself before going back in to soothe her. It's okay if your little one cries for short time with you in another room.<p dir=ltr>Don't be afraid to ask for help from a partner, a relative, a friend, a neighbor or a babysitter. And if you're frustrated and angry to the point of feeling the impulse to hurt your baby, get professional help in the form of a therapist or support group. If you or another caregiver may have shaken or hurt your child, even if it was brief or unintentional, call the doctor or go to urgent care right away.</p><br></div><div class="medical-authority py-4"><p>From the What to Expect editorial team and <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/about-heidi-murkoff/">Heidi Murkoff,</a> author of <em>What to Expect When You're Expecting</em>. 20 Arabic Baby Boy Names With Profound Meaning

by Omnia Gohar
Fact-Checked by Kathleen Felton

In search of a bold-sounding baby boy name with a powerful meaning? Let these Arabic baby boy names inspire you.

Arabic culture strongly believes that each name has a bearing on the character of its holder, which helps explains why almost every Arab name has a deep and often positive meaning. 

If you’re looking for a bold and beautiful name for your little bundle of joy, try on the following Arabic baby boy names for size. (And if you're not sure whether you're having a boy or a girl, check out our favorite Arabic baby girl names, too.)

1. Ali. This is one of the most common and timeless baby boy names in all Arab-speaking countries. Pronounced al-lee, the word ali literally means “high” or “elevated” — while the name itself means “noble, dignified, esteemed, well-respected.” Although it’s a strictly male name in the Arab world, Ali is a gender-neutral name in the U.S.

2. Amir. Meaning “prince,” Amir is a very common Arabic name that’s also widespread in the Hebrew and Persian languages — where it means “rich” or “prosperous.” Other Arabic meanings include “commander,” “chief,” and “powerful leader.” 

3. Eisa. The Arabic version of Jesus, this name remains very a top pick among Arab Muslims and Christians alike. In the Arabic language, the word "eisa," pronounced ee-sa, comes from the word "eise," meaning “a white camel with some blond hair.” You can also spell your little guy’s name Issa or Eissa.

4. Faris. Meaning “knight,” this beautiful and prestigious name (pronounced fa-res), is gaining popularity among Arabs. Faris can also mean “warrior” and is used to refer to someone who is well-versed, knowledgeable and highly experienced — promising a bright future on your little man.

5. Hamza. Don’t be fooled by how adorable this name sounds: It actually means “strong, unwavering.” No wonder, then, that the popularity of Hamza (also spelled Hamzah) is on the rise.

6. Hazem. From the word "hazm," meaning “seriousness,” Hazem translates as “strict, decisive, strong-willed.” Despite its serious meaning, the name has a variety of playful nicknames, including Mizo, Zooma, and Zoomy.

7. Ibrahim. In Arabic, this name means “the merciful father” — the Arabic alternative of Abraham. You’ll find the name Ibrahim across the Arab world; Hima is its sweet and well-loved nickname. 

8. Ismail. Often associated with hope and yearning, Ismail, pronounced es-ma-eil, literally translates to “God will listen.” And for good reason: The story behind this name dates back to Ibrahim (a prophet in the Islamic religion), who with his wife, Sarah, longed for a baby and prayed for years before they were given their son Ismail. 

9. Karim. Derived from the word "karam," meaning “generosity,” Karim (also spelled Kareem) means “generous, noble, virtuous.” Since the spirit of giving and generosity are core values of many Arabic cultures, the name is widely adored among Arab parents.

10. Mourad. Meaning “the desired,” “wanted,” or “wished,” it’s no wonder this super trendy name has long been a favorite of parents across the Arab world. 

11. Nadeem. While the word literally translates to “regretful,” this name actually means “close friend, companion, tactful, courteous.” The perfect name for your future bestie. 

12. Nour. Choose this moniker if you’re looking for a gender-neutral name that works equally well for both baby boys and girls. Nour means “light” or “luminescence” — a timeless and short-and-sweet choice.

13. Omar. Originally derived from the word "omor," meaning “time,” “age,” or “life,” Omar means “someone who enjoys a long life.” Throughout the years, it’s been the choice of many Arab families who hope their little ones live long and blessed lives. 

14. Ramy. This popular Arabic name, pronounced ra-me, has different meanings. It can mean “skilled at archery,” “determined,” or “pitcher.” The latter meaning is a home run if baseballers run in your family. 

15. Selim. Pronounced and alternately spelled Saleem, this trendy baby boy name means “safe, sound, and in good health.” Its meaning extends to a profound aspect beyond physical safety: having an intact heart and intentions.

16. Yaseen. This classic name continues to be a parental favorite today. Its exact meaning isn’t known: In fact, it’s mentioned in the Muslim’s holy book of Quran as one of several combinations of letters with a meaning that only God knows. 

17. Yunus. Also spelled (and pronounced) Younes, this gracious baby boy name is the Arabic form of Jonah. It’s derived from the Arabic verb "yu’nes," meaning “to keep someone company.” 

18. Yusuf. The Arabic version of Joseph, this baby boy name (which is pronounced and also spelled as Yousef) means “to receive multiplication of blessings by God.” Just like Joseph, the most common nickname for Yusuf is, you guessed it, Joe.

19. Zain. This light and lovely name for your little guy means “beautiful, graceful.” When combined with another name, Zain means “best of.” The feminine form of the name is Zainah, making Zain (also spelled Zane or Zayn) a common gender-neutral name in Arabic countries including Saudi Arabia. 

20. Ziyad. A beautiful and popular baby boy name that means “abundance, extra, increase,” Ziyad (pronounced zee-yad) has a number of cool nicknames, including Zee, Zizo, and Zed. Arab families often opt for this name as a token of growth, goodness, and abundance of health and wealth for their newborn boys. 

Still looking for a baby name? Open the What to Expect for more ideas — plus get week-by-week updates on the tiny human you’re naming.

20 Beautiful Arabic Baby Girl Names

by Omnia Gohar
Fact-Checked by Kathleen Felton

Looking for a beautiful, unique, and meaningful name for your little lady? Take some inspiration from these popular Arabic baby girl names.

Deciding on a name for your baby girl can be both exciting and overwhelming: After all, it is one of the earliest and most influential decisions you make in your baby’s life.

If your name selection criteria include a feminine and beautiful-sounding name that will make your daughter stand out from the crowd, consider this list of trendy and popular Arabic baby girl names. (And if you're not sure whether you're having a boy or a girl, check out our favorite Arabic baby boy names, too.)

1. Alia. A prestigious name for your esteemed little girl, Alia, pronounced al-ya, literally translates to “high.” It’s used to describe an honorable woman or a girl who holds a high social standing and commands the respect and appreciation of everyone around her. Alternate spellings include Alya and Aliaa. 

2. Amira. Meaning “princess,” this lofty name has always been popular among Arab-speaking families. Miro is one of many adorable nicknames you could call your little lady. 

3. Aysha. This name comes from the Arabic word "aiysh," meaning “life.” Aysha means “full of life, vibrant, alive, and well.” Many families choose this timeless name as a token of a long and lucky life. 

4. Dima. Used in both Arabic and Russian, this dainty name has similar meanings in both languages. In Russian, it means “strong fighter,” while in Arabic, it means “continuous, enduring, and everlasting.” It can also translate as a pleasant rain without thunder or lightning. 

5. Farida. Often associated with sophistication and social status, this elegant name was held by Queen Farida of Egypt in the 40s. Pronounced fa-reeda, it literally translates to “unique” — a lovely salute to your one-of-a-kind gal.  

6. Farrah. This gorgeous baby girl name, pronounced far-rah, means “joy, happiness” and is a timeless, go-to choice among Arabic families. What more perfect way to celebrate your little bundle of joy?

7. Jamila. There’s no wonder why this name remains popular in almost all Arab-speaking countries: It means “beautiful.” Derived from the Arabic noun "jamal" (which has the same meaning), Jamila describes beauty in both looks and character. You might just call your cutie Gigi for short.  

8. Layan. Its meaning is as delicate and sweet as it sounds: “soft, delicate, and tender.” A widespread name in many Arab countries — especially in Lebanon, Jordan and Syria — you could also call your sweetie by the common nickname Lily.  

9. Mariam. Also spelled (and pronounced) Maryem, Mariam is the Arabic form of the biblical name Miriam. While the name’s origins can be traced back to many languages and religious references, it refers to a woman who is admired for her devotion and helpfulness — characteristics we all hope for in our little ones.

10. Miral. Originating from Turkey, this name means “small gazelle.” Despite its Turkish origins, this charming name is gaining popularity in the Arab world. You can call your baby Mira for short. 

11. Nadia. Traditional yet trendy, Nadia is derived from the word "nada," meaning “morning dew” and is used to describe a generous and a natural giver. Such a light and pretty name for your baby girl! 

12. Nadine. Here’s a sweet cross-cultural choice: Nadine’s origin can be traced back to several languages, including French, Greek, and Russian, where it means “hope.” In the Arabic language, this popular name translates to “bearer of good news, messenger of blessings.” 

13. Nour. You simply can’t go wrong with this name, which means “light” or “luminescence.” It’s timeless, gender-neutral, and short and sweet. 

14. Rayya. This baby girl name, pronounced rye-ya, sounds lovely — and has an even lovelier meaning. While Rayya literally translates to “satisfied thirst,” “green leaves,” or “fragrant breeze,” it refers to a woman who lives a life of prosperity, with all her needs quenched.

15. Salma. Common in both the Arab world and in Spain, this exquisite name means “safe, well, and sound.” It comes from the Arabic word "salam," meaning “peace.” 

16. Sofana. One of the most authentic Arabic names, Sofana is derived from the word "sawfa," meaning “will happen.” The name itself means “patient, calm, tolerant, and willing to endure.” Sofy would be a cute nickname. 

17. Tala. This baby name’s popularity has been on the rise across Arab countries for the past couple of years — not only because it’s easy to pronounce and write, but also because it means a “beautiful palm tree” in Arabic and a “beautiful and youthful lady” in Greek.

18. Tia. Despite its popularity in many Arab countries in recent years, the origin of Tia, pronounced tee-ya, can be tracked to several languages. In Greek, it means “princess,” and in Spanish it means “aunt.” In Arabic, Tia refers to delicacy and femininity. 

19. Yasmeen. Props to you if you already guessed it: Yasmeen means “jasmine flower.” This sweet Arabic name withstands the test of time, remaining a favorite baby girl name throughout Arabic countries. 

20. Zainah. A popular Arabic name that means “pretty, lovely, or gorgeous,” zainah can also mean “decoration.” As a name, Zainah (pronounced zane-nah) refers to a girl or a woman who is “decorated” by her graciousness and good manners.  

Still looking for a baby name? Open the What to Expect for more ideas — plus get week-by-week updates on the tiny human you’re naming.

8 Things to Keep in Mind When Choosing a Baby Name

by Kathleen Felton
Fact-Checked by Catherine Donaldson-Evans

Need baby name help? Get advice on choosing a name for your baby-to-be from members of the What to Expect community.

Some parents have their baby's name picked out before their child is even conceived, while others wait until after their baby is born (and about to be discharged from the hospital!).

If you're agonizing over all the choices out there and need baby name help, you're far from alone. Below, tips on choosing a baby name for your little one from What to Expect parents who have been there.

Key Takeaways

Think about sound, meaning, and practicality when naming your baby. Consider how the name flows, possible nicknames, initials, and the significance or cultural/ethnic meaning behind it.

Balance tradition and originality: You might choose to honor family names or traditions, but don’t shy away from uncommon or unique choices if you prefer; also check popularity if originality matters to you.

Let the baby inspire their name if needed: Some parents wait until birth to see which name truly fits their child, allowing their little one’s personality to guide the final choice.

1. Make it sing

Consider the cadence, and be careful about combinations that could turn your child's name into a joke.

2. Consider nicknames

Make sure you're happy with both the long and short versions of your child's name (e.g. Nate for Nathaniel, Katie for Katherine) because he or she may pick up the nickname whether you like it or not.

"You can’t always control how other people will give a nickname, but you can always use his full name and introduce him that way in hopes that people will follow suit," says What to Expect Community member mergirl2325.

3. Look at initials

If you like the way C.J. sounds, Carl Joseph might be a good combo for your baby-boy-to-be. Or, you might choose to avoid certain initial combinations that you don't love as much.

"My daughter’s initials are EMW… but middle names aren’t really used much so really it’s EW. We thought about it and figured we liked the name too much," says What to Expect user kirstynwoah. "And if kids want to tease her they will find a way even if her initials were different."

4. Honor tradition

You might get creative with the way you use family names and contemplate combining them: his mom is Ann, yours is Mary — welcome little Ann Marie! Use your mother's maiden name, the name of a favorite relative, or a passed-down family name as either a middle or first name.

"We’re looking to combine the names 'Marian' and 'Martha' into a girl’s name and so far we’ve come up with Maren," says What to Expect user CeeJay2012.

5. Don't be afraid to try something new

There's nothing wrong with an uncommon name!

6. Consider what's popular now

Often, a parent hears a name he or she likes — the lead character from a TV show or the heroine of a novel — only to discover that, er, everyone else likes that name, too. If originality is important to you, check out the top girl names and top boy names to see if your choice shows up (and then choose something else!).

7. Analyze the meaning

Parents often choose a baby name by picking one with a special meaning or association. For example, you may feel so-so about "Bryan" until you learn it means strength and honor. Another source of inspiration is the ethnicity and/or its historical associations (a president, famous artist or explorer). 

"We named our son Jayden for the meaning behind it — it's a Hebrew name meaning: God has answered your prayers," says What to Expect user chachymom.

8. See what fits

If all else fails, look to your new family member for help. Parents-to-be who can't decide on a name might simply want to wait until their baby is born. 

"With [son] Aidan I went through three major phases," says What to Expect member Gidgetgirl. "First he was Caleb. Then it was Joshua. On the way to the hospital I said 'I really like Aidan' and we went with it after he was born. It just fit."

Still debating the perfect baby name? Open the What to Expect app for the top 1,000 names — plus tips for naming your baby from parents who have been there too.

Searching for a Dashing Baby Boy Name? These 15 British Boy Names Deliver

by Kim Conte
Fact-Checked by Jennifer Kelly Geddes

Fact-Checking Standards
