Searching for a cute and unique baby girl name? Look no further. From Cassia to Inez, you'll find the perfect name for your little girl on this list.

Want to find a truly unique baby name that your little girl won't share with any other kids in her playgroup? These one-of-a-kind baby girl names deserve your consideration.

1. Amelie. Though it might remind you of the whimsical French film Amelie, this is an original (French) take on the name Amelia, meaning "hard-working."

2. Aria. A strong name for a strong little girl, this is the Italian form of Ariel, meaning "lioness of God."

3. Bette. Calling to mind the actresses Bette Midler and Bette Davis, this is one of a number of unique midcentury names that's sure to come back in vogue. It's the French version of Betty, meaning "consecrated to God."

4. Calla. You'll be reminded of the pretty lily so often seen at weddings. Or go a little Greek with the unusual name Calliope, the muse of epic poetry also meaning "beautiful voice."

5. Cassia. For your feisty girl, this Greek name is a cinnamon-like spice.

6. Clementine. This sweet fruit also means "merciful" in Latin. You could call her Clem for short.

7. Effie. This Greek name means something we all hope for in our kids: "well spoken of." It can also be short for Alfreda or Euphemia.

8. Eva. This name was popular back in the 1890s. It's short for Evangelina (Greek), "bearer of good news," or a variation on Eve (Hebrew), meaning "life."

9. Greta. The 1920s actress Greta Garbo probably comes to mind; this name is actually short for Gretchen — a German form of Margaret.

10. Harlow. A play on the popular last name trend (think gorgeous blond star Jean Harlow of the 1930s), this name means "protector of the people."

11. Inez. A Spanish twist on Agnes — a trendy name 100 years ago — this baby girl's name is Greek for "pure."

12. Kaia. This short and sweet name means "earth" in Greek.

13. Luella. A familiar form of Louise, this powerful twist on the English moniker means "famous warrior."

14. Mae. A variation on "May" that's not seen so often these days, this name hit the top 100 around the early 1900s. (And Mae Jemison was the first African American woman in space!)

15. Melina. This Greek name means "honey."

16. Naya. This airy little girl's name could be short for the Basque name Nayara, meaning "swallow."

17. Poppy. A punchy yet pretty little girl's name with character, this flower name has lots of cute variations — Popee, Popi, Poppie, Poppea.

18. Quinn. Another take on the last name trend (think comedian Colin Quinn), this powerful, gender-neutral name means "queen" in German and English.

19. Sia. This unique little girl's name is so powerful, the Australian singer goes by it alone. It could also be short for the Irish name Sianna ("God is gracious").

20. Vega. Popular in Scandinavia, this unique gender-neutral name means "falling star."

21. Vera. The designer Vera Wang commonly pops up as inspiration for this girl name. Meaning "true" or "faith" and short for Elvera and Veronica in in Latin and Slavic, Vera was actually among the SSA's top 100 in the 1920s.

22. Zinnia. This cousin to the sunflower has bright fuchsia, yellow, red, and orange flowers as vibrant as your little girl.

23. Zosia. If you're a fan of the TV show Girls, you probably think of Zosia Mamet when you hear this baby name. It's also a close neighbor to the equally stunning Zósima, Greek for "vital, vigorous."

24. Zuri. Swahili for "beautiful," this is a gorgeous and unique baby girl name.

Choosing “the one” is no small feat. Find more names you’ll love in the What to Expect app — plus get week-by-week updates on the tiny human who’ll soon wear that name proudly.

25 Unisex Baby Names You'll Love

by Alyssa Sparacino
Fact-Checked by Kathleen Felton

Fact-Checking Standards

Searching for the perfect gender-neutral name for your little one? Check out the top unisex baby names here.

These days, gender reveals are an increasingly popular way to find out your baby's sex and announce it to the world. But if you’re one of those parents who would prefer to be surprised in the delivery room rather than in front of friends and family while cutting cake, these unisex names will save you a lot of in-the-moment deliberation and stress.

Plus, you might be surprised: Many monikers that have traditionally been thought of as a boy or girl name make a great gender-neutral name, too. You’ll love seeing how so-called boy’s names work for a baby girl, and vice versa — sometimes all it takes is one creative parent (or a famous celebrity) to change the perspective.

Here, some of our favorite unisex baby names for a baby boy or a baby girl. You can't go wrong with any of these gender-neutral ideas.

1. Alex

The variations of this classic unisex name can be written a few different ways on your child's birth certificate: Alex is, of course, a go-to nickname for Alexandra and Alexander, but it can also be shortened from Alexis, Alexia, Alexa, or Alexandria — or simply opt for Alex on its own.

2. James

You might not have considered the name James as being gender-neutral until actress Blake Lively gave her daughter the name in 2017. Nicknames like Jim or Jimmy work well for a boy, while Jamie is a sweet option for a girl.

3. Blake

Much like her daughter, Blake Lively knows what it’s like to navigate the world with a unisex name. Blake is a popular unisex name for both boys and girls, landing number 265 on the Social Security Administration's (SSA) list of top names in 2024 for boys, and 210 the same year for girls.[1]#1

4. Kyle

Real Housewives fans will instantly recognize where the inspiration for this unisex baby name comes from: Kyle Richards of the Beverly Hills cast.

5. Drew

Drew Barrymore, Drew Carey, Drew Brees. This four-letter name is easy to pronounce, easy to spell and easy to choose, whether you're expecting a boy or a girl.

6. Taylor

Another old-school favorite unisex baby name that has stood the test of time. Not only does the name Taylor work for both girls and boys, but it’s a common surname, too.

7. Kennedy

Although currently more popular for girls than boys — the name took spot 89 on the SSA's 2024 list for girls, but was not in the top 1,000 for boys — Kennedy is a noble name perfect for a natural-born leader.

8. Jordan

Jordan is a classic gender-neutral baby name, nabbing spot 539 in 2024 for girls and 104 for boys. Celebrities like Jordan Sparks and Jordan Peele come to mind.

9. Parker

Parker is one of those charming gender-neutral names that works just as well in the baby years as it does into adulthood. Plus, it sounds perfect alongside basically any middle or last name.

10. Avery

This unisex baby name was one of the most popular names for girls in 2024, landing spot 31, but works equally well for boys (it nabbed spot 259 that same year).

11. Ryan

Ryan might seem like a boy’s name, but it's become more popular over the past few years for baby girls. You can also choose an alternate spelling, such as Rhyan or Ryann.

12. Brooklyn

Brooklyn Decker rocks her name, and Brooklyn Beckham sure does, too. This location-inspired name is a no-brainer.

13. Cameron

Cameron Diaz is one famous Cameron, but this unisex baby name works also works well for boys. Plus, the nickname Cam couldn’t be cuter.

14. Logan

Although often thought of as a boy’s name, Logan is absolutely a unisex baby name that has an equally nice ring for any lucky little girl.

15. Emerson

Perhaps this baby will be a creative like his or her philosopher namesake: Ralph Waldo Emerson. Consider this unisex baby name if you envision raising a free thinker.

16. Charlie

More and more, this now-unisex baby name is being used for girls. Think: Rebecca Romijn’s daughter with husband Jerry O'Connell. Charly or Charley are sometimes used as alternate spellings.

17. Ezra

This unisex baby name also made our list of the top hipster baby names, and for good reason. Ezra works perfectly for a boy or girl, is easy to spell and blends seamlessly with many middle or last names.

18. Austin

Another city-inspired unisex baby name, Austin is a great choice for a girl or boy — living in Texas not required.

Still hunting for the perfect baby name? Open the What to Expect app for the top 1,000 names (and plenty of unique ones, too) — plus get week-by-week updates on the tiny human you’re naming.

50 Vintage Baby Names That Are Making a Comeback

by Whitney C. Harris
Fact-Checked by Kathleen Felton

Antique names like Rosemary and Hank will stand the test of time.

Picking a name for your baby-to-be is one of the biggest, most permanent decisions that moms and dads have to make on the journey to parenthood. Some expecting parents like to buck tradition when it comes to naming their new bundle of joy, coming up with uncommon monikers like Crispin or Reverie. Others take to trendy, hipster names that sound cool and feel very of-the-moment, like Axel, Presley, or Wyatt.

Still others find that relying on traditional names is a safe bet when it comes to choosing a baby name that will truly stand the test of time. But even these conventional options have been gaining popularity recently.

The U.S. government has taken notice by releasing a list of the top 1,000 names for boys and girls that have become much more common in the past few years. Trusted SourceSocial Security AdministrationTop 10 Baby Names of 2024See All Sources [1] Among the group are some vintage baby names that you might not have considered if you're currently scouring modern naming books and sites. A classic, old-fashioned baby name that was popular in decades past may strike the perfect balance between modern sensibilities and time-honored traditions.

Eager to see what's making the rounds? Here are some of the top vintage baby names for boys and girls that are rising in the charts. Vintage baby names may not be right for everyone, but it's good to know which ones are making a comeback!

17 Trendy Yet Timeless Welsh Baby Boy Names You’ll Cherish

by Lauren Cocking
Fact-Checked by Jennifer Kelly Geddes

Fact-Checking Standards

Getty Images
You might be surprised how many of today’s trendy names have Welsh roots. Take some inspiration from these fresh, classic, and bold Welsh baby boy names.

Classic-sounding and easy to spell, these adorable Welsh monikers are short and sweet with cute meanings to boot.

Whether you like softer, trendier “-i” endings, bold single-syllable names, or solid and strong-sounding options with ancient roots, there’s surely a Welsh baby boy name to suit you and your soon-to-be-born son. (And if you're not sure whether you're having a boy or a girl, check out some of our favorite Welsh baby girl names too.)

Looking for more charming baby names? Explore the What to Expect app and find thousands of sweet options to browse, save, and share.

  1. Aron. A variant of the Hebrew name Aaron, Aron is the Welsh spelling; it feels both modern and sophisticated. Music fans? It was also Elvis Presley’s middle name.
  2. Bowen. Although it sounds contemporary, due to its growing popularity in the U.S., Bowen is actually an ancient Welsh name meaning “son of Owen.” Bowen can be shortened to the very adorable Bo. 
  3. Bryn. It's often used for both boys and girls in the U.S., but Bryn is usually a boy’s name in Wales that means “hill."
  4. Cai. Here’s a multicultural option for you: Cai (or Kai or Caio) is a simple but trendy name that’s popular not only in Wales but also in China and parts of Europe — making it a fantastic option for families with roots around the world. In some countries, it’s considered more feminine than masculine.
  5. Deri. Strong in both sound and meaning, Deri is the plural of the Welsh word for “oak tree.” Uncommon in Wales, Deri is a cute but underrated name.
  6. Dylan. Popular across the British Isles — especially in Wales, where it originates — Dylan means “son of the sea” — ideal for water-loving parents and would-be water babies.
  7. Elis. Unisex in other parts of the world, Elis is a boy’s name meaning “kind” in Wales. With a soft “s” ending and the popular letter “e” start, Elis is quite trendy right now.
  8. Emyr. Delicate and lyrical, Emyr is the perfect name for your little “king” — one that’s relatively unheard of outside of Wales. Any little one would be lucky to get such a sweet and strong name.
  9. Geraint. If you’re a fan of history and folklore, there are few better names than the bold and strong-sounding Geraint, a warrior-king in Arthurian legend.
  10. Gethin. Gethin, meaning “dark and swarthy,” sounds soft and gentle thanks to that central “th.” If your baby boy is born with a dark head of hair, keep Gethin in mind!
  11. Harri. Also popular in Finland, Harri is a cute variant of the popular and princely British name Harry — itself a nickname for Henry. Appropriately, it means “ruler.”
  12. Huw. The Welsh version of Hugh, the classic yet modern boy’s name Huw is due for a comeback. Plus, it rather beautifully means “soul” or “intellect.”
  13. Idris. Recently recognizable thanks to actor Idris Elba, classy Idris is both a Welsh and Arabic boy’s name that’s also the name of a Welsh mountain, Cadair Idris.
  14. Morgan. More commonly a feminine name in the U.S., the unisex Morgan remains popular for Welsh boys. Possible meanings include “ruler of the sea” and “magic.”
  15. Osian. Lyrical and soft, gentle Osian (pronounced osh-an) derives from the Irish poet-warrior Oisín and means “little deer.”
  16. Rhys. Sometimes anglicized to Reece or Rees — or feminized to Reese — Rhys is a sweet and classic Welsh name that remains popular to this day.
  17. Siôn. Both a first and surname — and the Welsh equivalent to the John (English) and Seán (Irish) — Siôn means “God is gracious.” The female version is Siân; both versions can be written with or without the circumflex.

Cute, Quirky, and Easy to Say: 19 Adorable Welsh Baby Girl Names

by Lauren Cocking
Fact-Checked by Jennifer Kelly Geddes

Popular in Wales, these sweet names are still under-the-radar in the U.S. Take some inspiration for your newest arrival from among these fresh Welsh baby girl names.

Often underrated and overlooked — especially in the U.S. — Welsh baby girl names are some of the cutest around. Not only do many of them end with the oh-so-popular "-i," they're typically short, sweet, and easy to pronounce.

As with Welsh baby boy names, even if you choose a longer name, there's likely to be a built-in nickname (or two) which will give your daughter options as she grows up.

Have a read through the following Welsh baby girl names, and remember that whichever one you choose, it'll sound fresh and feminine — and probably come with a super sweet meaning too!

Want to keep searching for the perfect baby name? Check out all the fun options in the What to Expect app.

  1. Alys. The Welsh twist on Alice, Alys (which you can also spell with an "i" — Alis) is simple but unique.
  2. Bethan. You guessed it: Bethan is an alternative to Bethany, minus the "-y" ending. Easy to spell and intuitive to pronounce, your daughter will thank you for giving her such a bold but pretty name.
  3. Cariad. The Welsh-language equivalent of "sweetheart" or "darling" as a term of endearment, Cariad is a strong name which offers a nice twist on the more common Carrie.
  4. Carys. From the Welsh "to love" — caru — Carys is an adorable name that means, unsurprisingly, "beloved." (It's also the name of Welsh actress Catherine Zeta-Jones' daughter.) Cerys is an equally lovely alternative spelling.
  5. Catrin. Catrin is bold and a touch sophisticated, while still leaving room for softer, more traditional nicknames like Cat and Kitty.
  6. Eira. Eira is the Welsh word for "snow" — and while it's one of the more uncommon names on the list, it's also incredibly delicate and an unusual alternative to current favorites like Emma and Ava.
  7. Eirlys. Eirlys, taken from the Welsh word for "snowdrop" and pronounced ire-liss, sounds just as delicate — and, thanks to the close-sounding iris, recalls the trend towards floral baby girl names. 
  8. Elen. Helen becomes Elen (or Elin) in Welsh, a chipper name originally derived from Greek meaning "sunshine" or "light." Elen was also the name of a Welsh saint.
  9. Enfys. Technically unisex but used more often for girls, Enfys (pronounced en-viss) means "rainbow" — making it the perfect name for parents expecting again after a loss.
  10. Ffion. Although the double "ff" might look confusing, it's pronounced like a single "f." Ffion is the Welsh version of an equally charming Gaelic name: Fiona.
  11. Gwen. Very popular in the 20th century, Gwen — as in Gwen Stefani — will have people going b-a-n-a-n-a-s over it again soon! Gwen is also a shortened version of Gwendolyn and related to the French name Guinevere.
  12. Lowri. If you like the names Laura and Lauren, Lowri is a quirkier Welsh alternative. Like those more popular variants, it also means "laurel."
  13. Mari. If you want a classic-sounding name that will stand the test of time, consider Mari — which is also common in Scandinavia and Eastern Europe.
  14. Meleri. A relatively unusual name with ancient roots but a modern sound, Meleri was a Welsh saint. You can shorten to Eleri and even Leri.
  15. Nia. Both Welsh and Swahili in origin, Nia offers a bold twist on the popular baby girl name Mia. Purposeful and strong, Nia also means "light" and is the Welsh form of Niamh, a common Irish name.
  16. Olwen. One of the more unique "-wen" names, Olwen has strong Lord of the Rings vibes without being a direct copy of the half-elven Arwen.
  17. Rhiannon. Rhiannon is a very popular girls name in Wales but relatively uncommon elsewhere. Lovely-sounding and lyrical, it can also be shortened to Rhian or Rhi. 
  18. Seren. Who doesn't want their little lady to shine bright? Seren, the Welsh word for "star," is a sophisticated-sounding girl's name that toes the line between popular and under-the-radar.
  19. Tegan. Almost unisex in sound, Tegan means "beloved" or "favorite" — perfect if you're planning on having just one child! You can also spell it the Irish way: Teagan.

16 Parents Share the One Thing They Wish They Had Known Before Choosing Their Baby's Name

by Maressa Brown
Fact-Checked by Kathleen Felton

Fact-Checking Standards

What to Expect follows strict reporting guidelines and relies on credible sources, such as peer-reviewed studies, academic research institutions, highly respected health organizations and experts in various fields. All content is fact-checked by professional journalists prior to publishing. 

We believe you should always know the source of the information you're reading. Learn more about our editorial and medical review policies.

 | September 28, 2025
Latest update:

Light copy updates and fact-checked for accuracy.

See more
Stocksy
"Don’t tell a soul your name until after the baby is born."

Choosing the perfect baby name can feel all at once thrilling and intimidating. After all, the name you give your little one will be an everlasting part of your child’s identity that they’ll carry with them forever.

Although many parents have a good deal of confidence in their baby name choice, it’s possible to have second thoughts. In fact, a survey conducted by Mumsnet.com found that nearly one-fifth of parents in the U.K. would choose a different name for their child if they could. The reason: 25% regretted their child’s name because it was “too commonly used,” while 21% said the name “just didn’t feel right.”

Even parents who don’t necessarily regret the name they chose say they wish they had foresight around certain challenges or even surprisingly positive twists and turns.

Here, 17 parents get real about the thing they wish they had known before landing on their baby’s name.

1. "After my sons were born, I wished there was a way to see LIVE data on what every other mom was naming their kids. I didn’t want to name my boys something that all other boys around their age were being named." — Anna L., Mankato, MN

2. “I wish I had thought about the way kids' speech develops. At 3 1/2 years old, most kids pronounce my son's name [Axel] as ‘A*****e,’ since the 'X' sound isn't mastered yet. My son says it as ‘Axel,’ since he's had lots of practice with that sound, but his preschool teachers must be cracking up all day long as the other kids shout ‘A*****e! A*****e!’ to get his attention. I’d still pick it, but I just would have been more prepared for all the toddler cursing.” — Jennifer F., Silver Spring, MD

3. “I wish I knew how many people would have baby name ‘suggestions.’ I once was asked by a woman at work what names I was considering. Then she responded with, ‘Ew, no, you really should consider...,’ and then proceeded to tell all the names she loved. I also wish I knew how much people have a need to shorten/abbreviate names. My daughter's name is Gracelyn — which we LOVE for its uniqueness — and people always ask us what we call her. ‘Uhhh, Gracelyn’ is usually my response.” — Jessica B., Annapolis, MD

4. “Don’t tell a soul your name until after the baby is born. I tested my daughter’s name out on a co-worker I wasn’t super close with, and her facial expression made me doubt everything. The few friends of mine who have announced the name of the baby ahead of time all have stories of at least one person who tries to convince them otherwise or tell them why they don’t like the name. It’s just rude.” — Margot D., Boston, MA

5. “I wish I’d known that you can change your mind up until you sign paperwork when you leave the hospital. It doesn't matter how many people you tell. Wish I stuck to my second thought/name which only came after we announced to family [but] before we left the hospital. My husband didn’t think we should change it since we already told people. There still may come a day when I go to the social security office to change it!” — Carolyne R., Philadelphia, PA

6. “I wish I’d known that people would tell you you are pronouncing your own child’s name wrong. My daughter’s name is Vera. We pronounce it to rhyme with Sara. Even after I tell people how we pronounce it, they like to tell me I have it wrong. ‘It should be like Veera and is ‘veering’ off the road.’ I then ask how they pronounce ‘aloe vera,’ and they still argue. I understand there may be two ways, but don’t tell me I’m wrong.” — Nicki W., Baltimore, MD

7. “I wish I’d known that I would feel so much pressure in choosing a name. Pressure to get it right. Pressure to make sure they loved it when they were older. Pressure of knowing that with one little name I was already starting to shape who they would be.” — Alicia A., South Bend, IN

8. “This might be silly, but I regret wasting middle names. We picked fun first names and honored grandparents with middle names, but now I’m wishing I’d just saved those family names in case our third is also a boy. If we keep having the same gender, we may run out of names we like.” — Allie M., Nashville, TN

9. “It is okay to pick a different name when you see your child. We had a completely different name picked out and then she was born, and it didn't fit.” — Alexann D., Wauwatosa, WI

10. “I wish I’d known that just because you love a name doesn’t mean your significant other will. [And] just because a name isn’t currently popular doesn’t mean it won’t become popular the same year your baby is born, and that’s okay.” — Autumn D., Jacksonville, FL

11. “Don't let your husband talk you into a name while you're still being sewn up after a C-section and are kind of out of it. I would have gone with a different name. And on that note, don't let people rush you into a name! My oldest was born in the morning, and we didn't name him until the evening. Nurses and family wouldn't let it go that we hadn't decided on a name! It's a lifelong decision, so it's okay to meet your little one — if you're undecided — and then pick a name. And it's okay go with a different name even if you already have a name on the nursery wall and monogrammed onesies and blankets.” — Becky D., Clover, SC

12. “As an adoptive mom, I didn’t choose my daughter’s first name. Now, I can't think of a more beautiful word. Anyway, I guess I wish I knew how much I could love a name I didn’t even choose myself!” — Becky B., Phoenix, AZ

13. “My two daughters and their friend were enjoying a late summer day at the neighborhood pool and were writing their initials on their snack cups. When my daughter realized that her initials — TRD —  'sound' like 'turd' I realized that perhaps my husband and I were remiss in thoroughly analyzing all aspects of our second daughter’s initials prior to naming her... Moral of the story: think about what the initials ‘sound’ like before naming your child.” — Kari D., Lake Wylie, SC

14. “My kids' names are spelled really similarly, even though to me, they are really different names. It wasn't until I wrote out all our names together on a greeting card that I realized how similar they are — and I was like, ‘What was I thinking!?’ I really wasn't going for matching names. So, sometimes I wish I had chosen names that were more different for them. But I still really like both names.” — Elena M., Cornwall-on-Hudson, NY

15. “I wish I'd known how mad my kids would get at me, because they have never ever once found their names on a coffee mug, keychain, other souvenir. They think it's a huge injustice, and I should have thought of this. I wouldn't have changed their names because of this though — in fact, it's kind of a positive because then I don't have to deal with them collecting all that stuff!” — Julie E., Orlando, FL

16. “I wish I had thought through alternative or non-traditional nicknames derived from the formal name. Our son is named ‘Isaac.’ And I’m happy with calling him ‘Ike’ for short, but it was luck that a doctor suggested it after we had named him.” — Ben H., Cleveland, OH

Still hunting for the perfect baby name? Open the What to Expect app for the top 1,000 names (and plenty of unique ones, too) — plus get week-by-week updates on the tiny human you’re naming.

20 Winter Baby Names for Your Little Snow Angel

by Colleen de Bellefonds
Fact-Checked by Kathleen Felton

Getty Images
Looking for a winter-themed name for your baby boy or girl? Check out these beautiful baby names inspired by snow, evergreen forests, and other seasonal motifs.

If your winter due date is fast approaching — or you just love the cheer of the season — a winter-inspired baby names will evoke the coziest time of year. Check out these winter names for your bundled-up bundle of joy.

  1. Aspen. Like the wintry Aspen tree and the posh Colorado ski resort, this English baby name works equally well for boys and girls.
  2. Branch. A Latin boy’s name for paw, claw, or tree branch — all reminiscent of a stroll through a wintry forest. And if you're a Trolls movie buff, you have another reason to choose this one!
  3. Clark. As in Griswald from the movie Christmas Vacation! Clark is a gorgeous, unisex baby name choice that means “cleric or scholar" in the French tradition.
  4. Eira. This pretty Welsh name for "snow" makes the perfect short-and-sweet choice for your little girl.
  5. Elsa. Meaning “noble” in German, this name is short for Elizabeth, or “consecrated to God,” in Hebrew. If you’re a Frozen fan, this is a gorgeous moniker for your little snow queen.
  6. Ember. This one conjures up images of a warm and toasty fire and is a unique choice for a fiery little girl. It's the French version of the English name Amber.
  7. Farr. We love this modern, jet-setter English boy’s name that means “traveler,” just like the three wise men. For a more formal-sounding variation, try Farren or Farron.
  8. Fraser. As in the fir tree, Fraser is a lovely baby name for a boy born in the winter months. You'll love the meaning even more: "strawberry" in French (“fraise”) or “curly-haired” in the English tradition.
  9. Holly. Nothing says holiday cheer like the name Holly. For a boy, try Hollis, which is an English name meaning "near the holly bushes."
  10. January. Actress January Jones may have made it famous, but it's still unique enough not to be too trendy.
  11. Izar. A one-of-a-kind Basque girl's name meaning “star,” like the Star of Bethlehem leading the three wise men. You might also like the variations Izarra or Izarre.

Browse baby names by style and origin with the What to Expect app.

  1. Lumi. A good choice for your little boy or girl that's the literal translation for “snow” in Finnish.
  2. Mac. The baby name Mac pays homage to the Maccabees, Jewish rebels celebrated each year at Hanukkah; Mac is also a Scottish name meaning "son."
  3. Nicholas. Jolly old St. Nick, the patron saint of kids, inspires this baby name. It means "victorious people" in the Greek tradition.
  4. Neva. A baby girl name in the Spanish tradition for snow (nieve) — or “new” in English — this is also a river in Russia near St. Petersburg.
  5. Noel. Another holiday-inspired moniker, this French baby girl and boy name (often spelled "Noelle" for a girl) means "day of Christ’s birth."
  6. Olwen. This pretty Welsh baby girl’s name means “white footprint” — a lovely image for a snowy winter day.
  7. Vale. Although Vail is the name of the popular winter skiing destination, this alternate gender-neutral spelling English name also brings to mind wintry scenes and means "valley."
  8. Wynter. This super cool baby name, meaning “winter” in the English tradition, works equally well for a little boy or girl snow bunny. Cute nickname: Wynn!
  9. Yule. If you love Christmas-sounding names, "yule" love this unique unisex name. It’s English for "born at Christmas.”

dir=ltr>A humidifier may not top your <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/baby-products/registry/best-baby-registries rel="">baby registry</a>, but it can be a real comfort during dry winter months — especially when sniffles strike. As a mom of four, I’ve learned to keep mine close by whenever my little ones are under the weather. It’s amazing how much easier everyone sleeps (and breathes!) with a little extra humidity in the air.<p dir=ltr>The best baby humidifiers quietly add moisture to help ease congestion and keep sensitive skin from drying out, sans noisy gurgles or steamy surprises. “Ideally, a baby’s room should have 30 to 50% humidity,” says <a href=https://www.northwell.edu/find-care/find-a-doctor/dr-dyan-sharone-hes-md-11516601 target=_blank rel="">Dyan Hes, M.D</a>., a pediatrician at Northwell Lenox Hill Hospital. If the air feels desert-dry, a humidifier can help bring it back to that comfy sweet spot. <p dir=ltr>Of course, there are plenty of factors to consider before buying a humidifier. You'll want to think about the type, ease of cleaning, and coverage area, for starters. And if it happens to look good in baby’s space, too, even better! Here’s how I picked the best baby humidifiers — with expert insight and parent feedback from What to Expect's community leading the way.<h2 dir=ltr>How I Chose the Best Baby Humidifiers</h2><p dir=ltr>To make sure these picks were both safe and practical, I not only spoke with Dr. Hes, but several other pediatricians and sleep experts as well, including: <ul><li data-start=1514 data-end=1579><a href=https://mdmercy.com/find-a-doctor/emily-wisniewski-md target=_blank rel="">Emily Wisniewski, M.D.</a>, a pediatrician with Mercy Family Care Physicians in Baltimore, Maryland<li data-start=1514 data-end=1579><a href=https://www.pediatrics.columbia.edu/profile/lauren-d-levine-md target=_blank rel="">Lauren Levine, M.D.</a>, a pediatrician affiliated with NewYork-Presbyterian/Columbia University Irving Medical Center and NewYork-Presbyterian Morgan Stanley Children's Hospital<li data-start=1514 data-end=1579><a href=https://www.mcw.edu/education/medical-school/people/ellen-m-schumann-md-ms-faap target=_blank rel="">Ellen M. Schumann, M.D.</a>, a clerkship director at the Medical College of Wisconsin<li data-start=1514 data-end=1579><a href=https://www.hopkinsallchildrens.org/Find-A-Doctor/Practitioner-Details/Luis--Enrique--Ortiz target=_blank rel="">Luis E. Ortiz, M.D.</a>, a physician in the Sleep Center at Johns Hopkins All Children’s Hospital<li data-start=1514 data-end=1579><a href=https://www.connecticutchildrens.org/doctors/melanie-sue-collins-md target=_blank rel="">Melanie Sue Collins, M.D.</a>, medical director of the Division of Pediatric Pulmonary and Sleep Medicine at Connecticut Children's Medical Center<li data-start=1514 data-end=1579><a href=https://www.northwell.edu/find-care/find-a-doctor/pediatrics/dr-punita-ponda-md-11312728 target=_blank rel="">Punita Ponda, M.D.</a>, a New York-based Northwell Health physician who specializes in allergy and immunology and pediatrics</ul><p dir=ltr>Based on their guidance, in addition to feedback from parents in the What to Expect community, I ensured all of our selections met the following criteria:<ul><li dir=ltr><strong>Cool mist</strong>: The <a href=https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/at-home/medication-safety/Pages/How-to-Manage-Colds-and-Flu.aspx>American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends </a>using a cool mist humidifier over a warm mist one, as the latter could lead to accidental burns if knocked over. These are preferred by the AAP because warm mist humidifiers can pose a burn risk to baby. Cool mist humidifiers may also help to tamp down on microbial growth, says Dr. Wisniewski. “We get worried if there is warmth—this can be an environment that allows mold and other infectious bugs to grow,” she explains. <li dir=ltr><strong>Easy to clean</strong>: “It is important to clean and dry the tank and any parts that come in contact with water," says Dr. Levine. "Some tanks are designed to make this easier, others make it nearly impossible." Dr. Hes recommends changing the water and wiping the unit down daily, giving it a “good scrubbing with a brush” every week. (You can use vinegar and a toothbrush to get into any small crevices.) “This will ensure you clean out any mold or bacteria hiding in the humidifier,” Dr. Hes says. <li dir=ltr><strong>Automatic shut-off</strong>: “Since you usually run a humidifier at night while your baby is sleeping, you also should look for a machine with an automatic shut-off so that if the tank runs out of water it will turn off,” says Dr. Levine.<li dir=ltr><strong>Appropriate coverage</strong>: Too small and there will be no benefit; too big and you risk mold growth. Look at the model's recommended square footage when shopping to ensure it's compatible with the room you're planning to keep it in.<li dir=ltr><span id=docs-internal-guid-b765ca07-7fff-6924-3442-b420aaa0ebe8><strong>Directional flow</strong>: While not always necessary, having the option to point the mist where you want it to go is always a perk, says Dr. Schumann.</span></ul></div></div><div class="why-trust-us-section row no-gutters"><div class="col-12 col-sm-8 col-md-9 col-lg-10 why-trust-us-text-container"><h3 class=why-trust-us-title>Why Trust Us?</h3><p class=why-trust-us-text>What to Expect is the world’s most trusted pregnancy and parenting brand for a reason. It delivers an ultrafine, cool mist up to 40 inches high for even, room-wide hydration. The 1.6-gallon tank<strong> </strong>can run continuously for up to 60 hours in sleep mode, meaning fewer refills and more uninterrupted comfort. Despite its size, this humidifier operates at a near-silent 28 dB, making it ideal for nurseries.<p>Bonus: the top-fill design makes refilling and cleaning effortless, while the built-in humidity sensor automatically adjusts output. One WTE parent notes they love the modular design, making it easy to break down and clean. For extra peace of mind, the brand also separately sells a cartridge for descaling. The LED touch display lets you choose between three mist settings, set a timer (0–12 hours), or adjust the 15-degree nozzle for targeted misting. You can even add essential oils to the aroma tray for a calming touch or turn on the gentle night light to create a cozy bedtime glow.</div></div><div class=reviews><div class="community-reviews __tab-content d-md-block" data-product-id=best-humidifier-for-bigger-bedrooms id=communityReviews-best-humidifier-for-bigger-bedrooms><div class="community-reviews__title d-none d-md-block">Community Reviews</div><div class="community-reviews__list-swiper swiper-container"><ul class="community-reviews__list swiper-wrapper"><li class=swiper-slide><article class=community-review><div class=community-review__header><a class=community-review__author-link href=https://community.whattoexpect.com/forums/december-2023-babies/topic/humidifier-166191142.html> cmama510 </a> <span class=community-review__date></span></div><p class=community-review__body><div class=wte-reply__content><div class="wte-reply__content__message __messageContent fr-element fr-view"><p>"I got a dreo one when LO got sick. Same with their fans."</span></article></ul><div class=swiper-button-prev><svg class=naviation-arrow><use xlink:href=#left-arrow /></svg></div><div class=swiper-button-next><svg class=naviation-arrow><use xlink:href=#right-arrow /></svg></div></div></div></div></div><div class=how-we-chose-container><div class=how-we-chose-title><h3>What to Look for In a Baby Humidifier</h3></div><div class=how-we-chose-copy><p dir=ltr><span>There are a few factors to look for to make sure a baby humidifier will meet your needs. </span><ul><li dir=ltr><strong>Size</strong>: Each humidifier can only hold so much water. That’s why it’s important to look at the size of your baby’s room and the humidifier’s water tank capacity to make sure it will be able to distribute moisture throughout the night. Every product is different, but most 0.5 gallon tanks can push out moisture for 24 hours, while smaller and larger tanks will be able to go for longer. <li dir=ltr><strong>Adjustments and settings:</strong> While they’re not a requirement, features like LCD screens, smart technology, scheduled run times and automatic on-off settings can make operation of your baby humidifier a little easier. You may also want to consider ultrasonic vs. evaporative humidifiers. “Ultrasonic humidifiers are quiet and create a very fine mist,” says Dr. Hes. “An evaporative humidifier pushes the water through a wick and removes particles in the water this way.” <li dir=ltr><strong>Cleaning</strong>: Each humidifier has its own cleaning needs, making it important to read the manufacturer’s instructions carefully. Ultrasonic humidifiers can also turn bacteria and mold into a mist, making it important to follow the manufacturer’s instructions for cleaning, Hes says. The wick and filter must also be changed regularly in an evaporative humidifier “because they get very dirty,” Hes says. Dr. Wisniewski stresses the importance of being on top of cleanings. “From a safety perspective, you don’t want to have any sort of mold growth which would then be humidified through the air,” she says. “This can be dangerous because your child would be breathing it in. It is important to following the cleaning instructions on the box.”</ul><p><span id=docs-internal-guid-5cc923b2-7fff-f198-4834-33dfe8b8d48a></span></div></div><div class=faq-container><div class=faq__header><div class=faq__header__title><h2>FAQs</h2></div><div class=faq__header__line></div></div><div class="accordion faq-info-accordion" id=faqInfo><div class=card><div class=card-header><h4 data-toggle=collapse data-target=#question-5627-0 aria-expanded=false>Should I use a humidifier for my baby? <svg class="icon-collapse Chevron-Down"><use xlink:href=#Chevron-Down xmlns:xlink=http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink></use></svg> <svg class="icon-collapse Chevron-Up" style=display:none><use xlink:href=#Chevron-Up xmlns:xlink=http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink></use></svg></h4></div><div id=question-5627-0 class=collapse data-parent=#faqInfo><div class=card-body><p dir=ltr>The short answer is that it depends. But they can be helpful in certain climates and situations — the <a href=https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/at-home/medication-safety/Pages/How-to-Manage-Colds-and-Flu.aspx target=_blank rel="">AAP suggests using a humidifier</a> for baby if she <a href="https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/health-and-safety/colds-in-babies/" target=_blank rel="">has a cold</a>, for example.<p dir=ltr>“Benefits for using a humidifier in the nursery include protecting your child's skin from drying out and <a href=https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/at-home/medication-safety/Pages/How-to-Manage-Colds-and-Flu.aspx target=_blank rel="">decreasing nasal congestion</a>by helping loosen mucus — especially helpful if he or she is having a cold,” says Dr. Ortiz. “This can be a good thing, as there are limited over-the-counter remedies for children in this age group.” <p dir=ltr>Humidifiers could also help keep skin moist if your child has <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/baby-care/baby-skin-care/eczema.aspx rel="">eczema</a>, and could help keep nosebleeds at bay, says Dr. Schumann. <p dir=ltr>But you don’t necessarily need to use a humidifier for this, says Dr. Collins. “We have recommended passive humidification by placing aluminum lasagna pans filled with several inches of water in a place where the child cannot access them,” she says. “Then, changing the water and washing the pans in a dishwasher daily. Think about it, you can clean an open pan much easier than a closed humidifier.”<p dir=ltr>When deciding whether your child's room needs a dehumidifier, you need to make sure that it doesn't make the room too humid or too dry.<p dir=ltr>"Children, especially young children, if the air is too dry, will produce mucus," says Dr. Ponda. "You can't have it too warm, where it's too humid or too dry. So in a nursery, it's okay to have a dehumidifier, but you want to make sure it can regulate the humidity and it's not something that sucks humidity out of the air only."<p> </div></div></div></div><div class="accordion faq-info-accordion" id=faqInfo><div class=card><div class=card-header><h4 data-toggle=collapse data-target=#question-5627-1 aria-expanded=false>Where is the best place to put a humidifier in baby's room? <svg class="icon-collapse Chevron-Down"><use xlink:href=#Chevron-Down xmlns:xlink=http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink></use></svg> <svg class="icon-collapse Chevron-Up" style=display:none><use xlink:href=#Chevron-Up xmlns:xlink=http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink></use></svg></h4></div><div id=question-5627-1 class=collapse data-parent=#faqInfo><div class=card-body><p dir=ltr>The point of a humidifier might be to increase the humidity of a room, but you don't want a jet of mist hitting your child's face.<p dir=ltr>“As a general rule, you want to place it in an area where the mist can disperse easily through the air, but not accumulate moisture on surfaces such as the crib or ceiling,” explains Dr. Ortiz. After all, accumulation of moisture can encourage mold growth, which could make your little one sick.<p dir=ltr>You also want to make sure that the humidifier (and its cord!) are completely out of reach from your baby, says Dr. Levine. “You also do not want to place it on an elevated surface where your baby might pull it down on themselves.”<p dir=ltr>Keep in mind the size of the nursery, too. “If you put it in a room that is much smaller than it is meant for, you will end up with condensation on surfaces, which can be a breeding ground for microorganisms,” says Dr. Levine. On the other hand, if the humidifier is placed in a room that’s too big, it won't properly do its job.<p> </div></div></div></div><div class="accordion faq-info-accordion" id=faqInfo><div class=card><div class=card-header><h4 data-toggle=collapse data-target=#question-5627-2 aria-expanded=false>How and how often should you clean baby’s humidifier? <svg class="icon-collapse Chevron-Down"><use xlink:href=#Chevron-Down xmlns:xlink=http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink></use></svg> <svg class="icon-collapse Chevron-Up" style=display:none><use xlink:href=#Chevron-Up xmlns:xlink=http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink></use></svg></h4></div><div id=question-5627-2 class=collapse data-parent=#faqInfo><div class=card-body><p dir=ltr>"One thing that you have to worry about with use of humidifiers is the risk for increased exposure to bacteria and molds, as well as particulate matter and chemicals from cleaning the humidifier," says Dr. Ortiz. "These problems can be avoided by using distilled water, a humidifier with a filter and regular cleaning of the humidifier per the manufacturer's recommendations."<p dir=ltr>Keep in mind that some models require cleaning as often as every one to three days. Carefully read the instructions on your humidifier so you know how often yours should be cleaned.<p> </div></div></div></div></div><script type=application/ld+json>{"@context":"http://schema.org","mainEntity":[{"acceptedAnswer":{"@type":"Answer","text":"<p dir=\"ltr\">The short answer is that it depends. class="col-12 deck"><p dir=ltr>When your baby is all gums, it’s perfectly okay to use a damp cloth to clean her mouth. Once that first tooth breaks through the surface, however, it’s time to upgrade your teeth-cleaning gear. Of course, you’ll want to have the right <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/baby-products/baby-care/best-baby-toothbrushes>baby toothbrush</a>, but you’ll also want to make sure you’re equipped with the best baby toothpaste to keep her new pearly whites clean.<p dir=ltr>Toothpaste for babies, just like those made for adults, are designed to help remove plaque and bacteria from teeth and protect against cavities, explains <a href=https://www.rileychildrens.org/find-a-doctor/physician/laquia-a-walker-vinson target=_blank rel="">LaQuia Vinson</a>, DDS, MPH, a pediatric dentist with Riley Hospital for Children at Indiana University Health. But, before brushing baby’s teeth, you should know about some of the ways that your baby’s toothpaste may be different from your own.<h2 dir=ltr>How We Chose the Best Baby Toothpastes</h2><p dir=ltr>According to the <a href=https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/oral-health/Pages/Brushing-Up-on-Oral-Health-Never-Too-Early-to-Start.aspx target=_blank rel="">American Academy of Pediatrics</a> (AAP) and the <a href=https://www.aapd.org/media/policies_guidelines/p_fluorideuse.pdf target=_blank rel="">American Academy of Pediatric Dentists</a> (AAPD), the best baby toothpastes contain fluoride. That being said, you also want to find a toothpaste your baby will tolerate. To help narrow down your search, experts and What to Expect staff and community members say to consider the following factors when choosing the best baby toothpaste:<ul><li dir=ltr><strong>Age-appropriateness:</strong> When shopping for a baby toothpaste, the most important rule is to look for child-friendly toothpaste bearing the <a href=https://www.ada.org/resources/research/science-and-research-institute/ada-seal-of-acceptance target=_blank rel="">American Dental Academy (ADA) Seal of Acceptance</a>, even if the toothpaste's label says that the product is for kids aged 2 and up, Dr. Vinson says. In fact, many toothpastes marketed towards babies (often called "training toothpastes") aren't actually the best choice because they don't contain fluoride, which is important for keeping baby’s teeth strong and cavity-free.<li dir=ltr><strong>Flavor:</strong> Most tots tend to prefer fruity or bubble gum flavors, as many find mint-based flavors to be “spicy” or too strong. But if your munchkin happens to gravitate towards mint, there are a handful of kid-approved options out there that aren't as intense as mint flavors for adults. </ul><p>Each of the baby toothpaste on our list contains fluoride, is deemed safe for babies, and has received overwhelmingly positive reviews for baby tolerance among What to Expect staff and community members.</div></div><div class="why-trust-us-section row no-gutters"><div class="col-12 col-sm-8 col-md-9 col-lg-10 why-trust-us-text-container"><h3 class=why-trust-us-title>Why Trust Us?</h3><p class=why-trust-us-text>What to Expect is the world’s most trusted pregnancy and parenting brand for a reason. class=card><div class=card-header><h4 data-toggle=collapse data-target=#question-5418-0 aria-expanded=false>Do babies need fluoride toothpaste? <svg class="icon-collapse Chevron-Down"><use xlink:href=#Chevron-Down xmlns:xlink=http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink></use></svg> <svg class="icon-collapse Chevron-Up" style=display:none><use xlink:href=#Chevron-Up xmlns:xlink=http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink></use></svg></h4></div><div id=question-5418-0 class=collapse data-parent=#faqInfo><div class=card-body><p>Baby toothpaste should contain fluoride, per recommendations from the AAP and AAPD. Toothpaste that contains this mineral can help prevent cavities, rebuild tooth enamel and make sure teeth are as strong as possible, even in young mouths. If, however, you’re concerned about using fluoride, you can speak with your pediatrician or pediatric dentist to see what they recommend for your child.</div></div></div></div><div class="accordion faq-info-accordion" id=faqInfo><div class=card><div class=card-header><h4 data-toggle=collapse data-target=#question-5418-1 aria-expanded=false>When should I start using toothpaste for my baby? <svg class="icon-collapse Chevron-Down"><use xlink:href=#Chevron-Down xmlns:xlink=http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink></use></svg> <svg class="icon-collapse Chevron-Up" style=display:none><use xlink:href=#Chevron-Up xmlns:xlink=http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink></use></svg></h4></div><div id=question-5418-1 class=collapse data-parent=#faqInfo><div class=card-body><p><span id=docs-internal-guid-f7d00167-7fff-a265-4e54-0b55119f64dc>Start brushing your baby's pearly whites with toothpaste as soon as her first tooth erupts, says the AAP. Brushing as early as possible gives your little one maximum protection against cavities and sets the stage for a lifetime of good oral health habits. </span></div></div></div></div><div class="accordion faq-info-accordion" id=faqInfo><div class=card><div class=card-header><h4 data-toggle=collapse data-target=#question-5418-2 aria-expanded=false>What toothpaste is safe for babies? <svg class="icon-collapse Chevron-Down"><use xlink:href=#Chevron-Down xmlns:xlink=http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink></use></svg> <svg class="icon-collapse Chevron-Up" style=display:none><use xlink:href=#Chevron-Up xmlns:xlink=http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink></use></svg></h4></div><div id=question-5418-2 class=collapse data-parent=#faqInfo><div class=card-body><p dir=ltr>You may wonder if it’s okay to use your go-to formula when cleaning your little one's mouth. The answer: No. Babies need toothpaste designed specifically for young children, as “adult” formulas often have added ingredients such as whiteners and brighteners. Not only are these not safe for kids, but Dr. Vinson says they can be abrasive on your baby's gums. Plus, these formulas usually contain a high dose of fluoride that could actually damage your baby’s teeth or give them upset stomachs.<p dir=ltr>One important thing to note is that most kids’ fluoride toothpastes are labeled for ages 2 and up. But it's still safe — and in fact, recommended — to use these products for your baby, Dr. Vinson says.<p dir=ltr>So why the age discrepancy? Product labels haven't yet caught up <a href=https://www.aapd.org/globalassets/media/policies_guidelines/p_eccconsequences.pdf target=_blank rel="">with the latest research</a>. "In the past, the recommendation for children under age 3 was fluoride-free toothpaste," she explains. Now, studies show that the benefits of fluoride are important for children of all ages, and major medical organizations including the AAP and the AAPD say that infants and toddlers under 2 should use fluoride toothpastes.</div></div></div></div><div class="accordion faq-info-accordion" id=faqInfo><div class=card><div class=card-header><h4 data-toggle=collapse data-target=#question-5418-3 aria-expanded=false>How do I brush my baby's teeth? <svg class="icon-collapse Chevron-Down"><use xlink:href=#Chevron-Down xmlns:xlink=http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink></use></svg> <svg class="icon-collapse Chevron-Up" style=display:none><use xlink:href=#Chevron-Up xmlns:xlink=http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink></use></svg></h4></div><div id=question-5418-3 class=collapse data-parent=#faqInfo><div class=card-body><p dir=ltr>You should brush your baby's teeth twice a day, preferably after breakfast and before bedtime. <p dir=ltr>Use <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/baby-products/baby-care/best-baby-toothbrushes>an infant toothbrush</a> with soft or silicone bristles that will feel more comfortable in baby's mouth. You may be able to get the best leverage by sitting your baby on your lap facing away from you. Gently hold your baby's head with one hand, stabilizing the chin, and brush with the other hand.<p dir=ltr>Then, <a href=https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/teething/brushing-baby-teeth.aspx>gently brush in tiny circles</a> for about two minutes total. (Singing a song can help the time pass faster!) Brush her tongue too — just don't go too far back, since it can trigger gagging.<p dir=ltr>The AAP advises using a smear of toothpaste that’s about the size of a grain of rice. Move up to a pea-sized amount when your child is around age 3 and capable of spitting out the toothpaste after brushing.
